en: Preface to the Combined Edition of the Commentary on the Bodhisattva Precepts Sūtra:
My friend Master Yin has compiled this commentary on the sūtra. Having read it once, I praised it, saying:
"The characters are not erroneous and the sentences are not fragmented; its benefit to all beings is truly unsurpassed. However, this commentary was not explained by Jingxi [Zhiyi] himself.
Since the first four [chapters] clarify what is not explained in the subsequent sections, there is no need for a separate commentary (*caojì*); it is sufficient to rely entirely upon this work.

Thus, would it not also be appropriate to simply synthesize the sutra with its commentaries? Having heard this, Master Yīnggōng requested that it be placed at the beginning of the title, and he recorded these notes accordingly.
Preface by the Tiantai School Bhikṣu Weirenzi, in the late twelfth month of the Jiazi year of the Zhengxiang era.
Explanatory Commentary on the Meaning of the Bodhisattva Precepts Sūtra, Volume One.
Spoken by the Great Master Zhizhe of Tiantai during the Sui Dynasty.
Recorded by the Disciple Guanding.

Regarding the Bodhisattva Precepts: they are the initial chapter for directing one toward good and the foremost presentation for repelling evil. By returning directly to the Way, the source of rebirth can be exhausted.
If even the minor practices of the Śrāvakas are themselves held in precious esteem, how could a Mahāsattva of the *mokṣa* (liberation) not cherish them all the more?
By diligently upholding the precepts, both the internal and external paths are all reverently honored; the common people of the royal house offer their persons with devout respect.

This is the supreme cause for attaining the ultimate fruit and the wondrous karma for establishing the *maṇḍala*. However, regarding the characteristics of the precepts recorded in the sūtras and śāstras, there are many varieties;
as for the methods of receiving them explained in the records and traditions, there are certainly differences. This is truly because...
The capacities for awakening—whether partial or universal—and the suitability for detailed or concise expositions mean that words are not uttered in pairs and phenomena do not proceed simultaneously.
I have carefully examined the *dharmalakṣaṇa* (characteristics of phenomena) set forth by Master Kumārajīva, which originates from the "Chapter on the Vinaya Store" of the *Brahmajāla-sūtra*.

In the third year of the Hongshi era of the Qin dynasty, Master Kumārajīva arrived within the borders of Han and brought forth the Great Vehicle, rectifying and upholding the holy teachings, and translating sūtras and śāstras. III.
From among more than one hundred fascicles, this single volume of the *Brahmajāla-sūtra* was the last to be recited and brought forth.

Because he vowed to propagate and proclaim it, he repeated each word with earnestness three times over. This is because its literary expressions and meanings are profound and obscure, and its underlying intent is deep and mysterious;

therefore, he pointed it out as clearly as one’s palm to make it easy for future generations to attain awakening. It is called the *Brahmajāla* (The Brahma’s Net) because it seeks to clarify the various Buddha-dharmas.

The differences are like those described in the "Chapter on the Brahma-King’s Net. Regarding the term "mind-ground" (*cittabhūmi*), it refers to the Bodhisattva precepts which universally guard the three karmas.
While mind, thought, and consciousness are essentially one yet have different names, among the three karmas, mental karma is primary while bodily and verbal karma are secondary;
this is explained according to what is most eminent. Thus, it is called the "mind-ground. This scripture is interpreted through its three layers of profound meaning (*xuan-yi*).
First, the explanation of the name; second, the determination of the essence;
third, the analytical examination. Regarding the explanation of the name: first, the personal name is clarified; next, the designation of the dharma is distinguished;

finally, the stages and positions are explained. In the Sanskrit language of India, *mahā-bodhi-sattva*; now, when called "bodhisattva," the remaining characters are abbreviated, and it is translated as follows: [a being for enlightenment].

Those who have perfected the mind of the Great Way are called *sattvārtha-kārin* (Benefactors of Beings), also called *bodhisattva* (Awakening Beings), and further called those of "Excellent and Beautiful Courage.
They receive these names according to their conduct, for because they direct their minds with vast universality, they are established by this title.

The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* clarifies that such persons possess the mind of the Great Way which cannot be destroyed or shattered, being like a diamond (*vajra*), from the initial generation of the mind until the final attainment.
Those who attain equal enlightenment are all called Bodhisattvas and are also termed "Sons of the Buddha" (Buddhaputra), in the sense of succeeding to the lineage.

All three vehicles arise from the Buddha; thus, the understanding that they are all "sons" is complete. The *Lotus Sūtra* states: "If one is like my son, the Mahāsattva who succeeds to the lineage is superior and is called a 'true son'.
Furthermore, since those of the two vehicles likewise cultivate the path, they all possess this status as sons.

The path from self-realization to the minor fruits is narrow and short, whereas that of the Mahāsattva is broad and long; because he realizes himself and enables others to realize themselves, he receives this title.
As a great sūtra says: "From the first aspiration, one is already a teacher for humans and devas, surpassing both śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas"—therefore, it is called the "Great Mind."

Next, we shall distinguish the designation of this dharma, which is the meaning of *śīla*. The Sanskrit term *śīla* is translated in the Qin language as "innate goodness" (*xing shan*) and also as "cooling" (*qing liang*).
It is so named because it can arrest the heat and affliction of breaking the precepts; it is thus designated according to its function.

It is also called *pratimokṣa*, translated as "guarantee of liberation" (*bao jie tuo*); it is further termed "pure livelihood" (*jing ming*), and is also said to be "the accomplishment of dignified deportment" (*chengjiu wei yi*).

Having nothing to receive or store, one is free from future places of birth and the three evil realms; one receives a physical form in a pure land, can cease wrong livelihoods, and guards against non-virtue by stopping evil.
Furthermore, it is said that "precept" (*śīla*) has the meaning of "restraint," the meaning of "training," and the meaning of "binding.
All these names are established according to their respective meanings. As the Great Sūtra says: "If you still speak of impermanence despite the Buddha’s prohibition, then..."
If one breaks the Buddha’s prohibitions regarding the tongue, one will fall into ruin. It is further said that such a person’s observance of all precepts is incomplete;

they cannot even attain the enlightenment of the Two Vehicles, let alone the Unsurpassed Way. Now, as for what is called "precept" (*śīla*), there are the precepts of restraint (*saṃvara-śīla*), the precepts concurrent with meditative concentration (*dhyāna-sahaja-śīla*), and the precepts concurrent with the Path (*mārga-sahaja-śīla*). These names originally derive from the Tripiṭaka Vinaya; "vinaya" refers to the rules of restraint.

Because physical deportment can restrain the various evils of the body, it is called "precept" (*śīla*) and also termed "dignified demeanor" (*airyāpatha*). "Dignity" (*airya*) means pure, solemn, and awe-inspiring;

"demeanor" (*patha*) means a model for practitioners, such that they are reverent and awe-struck. It is also called "taming and guiding," which means making the mental activities harmonious and virtuous.
"Concentration" (*samādhi*) means stillness and withdrawal; at the time of entering concentration, one naturally becomes harmonious and virtuous, preventing all [distractions].
"Evil" refers to the path that can thoroughly manifest the truth; after this, one naturally ceases to commit transgressions.
When cultivating the field of the first fruit (*srotāpanna*), insects are moved four inches away; this is the power of the "path shared" (*mārga-sādhāraṇa*).

Since these two precepts are the superior functions of the mind, they can give rise to both the path of morality (*śīla-mārga*) and meditative concentration (*samādhi*), arising simultaneously with the restraint (*saṃvara*); therefore, they are called "shared. The Sarvāstivādins explain this as "restraint" (*vinaya*).
The precepts of dhyāna and the untainted precepts (anāsrava-śīla)—though these names originate from the Tripiṭaka, the excellent bodhisattva precepts likewise possess these three names.

If they are obtained through formal vows, they are termed "restraint" (saṃvara). If they are associated with the meditative concentration of a bodhisattva or the path, they all generally refer to "precepts" (śīla) as they restrain the three types of action.
As for the restraint of conduct, the gathering of wholesome dharmas, and the gathering of sentient beings—these...
The name "Threefold Aggregate of Precepts" (tri-skandha-śīla) originates from the *Bhūmi-samudra-saṃgraha* and does not apply to the Tripiṭaka;

the "Great Being’s Discipline" (mahāsattva-vinaya) encompasses both restraint (*saṃvara*) and non-restraint (*asaṃvara*). Regarding the three types of action, those manifested through body and speech are all termed "discipline" (*vinaya*).

As for "gathering wholesome qualities" (*kuśala-dharma-saṃgrāhaka*), based upon discipline, one gives rise to the great bodhicitta, which can restrain all unwholesome non-practices and diligently cultivate all virtues until they are perfected.
The Bodhisattva vow that encompasses the salvation of beings consists of eleven matters by which a Bodhisattva benefits sentient beings;

these are all ways of benefiting things and extensively aiding sentient beings. Having extensively enumerated all the precepts of a Bodhisattva in the Chapter on Precepts, the nine types of precepts are here summarized as being subsumed within the three types of precepts:
the *saṃvara* (restraint) precept, which enables the mind to abide; and the *kuśaladharma-saṃgrāhaka* (gathering of wholesome dharmas) precept, by which one accomplishes the good for oneself.

The "Dharma of the Buddha" (*buddhadharma*), "gathering and sustaining beings" (*sattvaparigraha*), and "accomplishing sentient beings" (*sattvasampādana*): these three encompass all the precepts of a Mahāsattva. The *Ratnakūṭa Sūtra* (*Yingluo jing*) states:

"The precept of restraint" (*saṃvara-śīla*) refers to the ten *pārājikas*; "the precept of gathering wholesome qualities" (*kuśaladharma-saṃgrāhaka-śīla*) refers to the eighty-four thousand Dharma-gates;

and "the precept of gathering and sustaining beings" (*sattvaparigraha-śīla*) refers to transforming sentient beings through loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity, causing them to attain peace and happiness. (From the "Chapter on Precepts" in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*).

The ten kinds of precepts are enumerated as follows: first, unimpaired; second, unbroken; third, unpierced; fourth, unmixed; fifth, conforming to the Path; sixth, unattached; seventh, praised by the wise;
eighth, sovereign; ninth, conforming to meditative concentration; and tenth, complete. Inferring the meaning of these ten:
"unimpaired" refers to upholding the natural precepts (*prakṛti-śīla*). Being fundamentally pure and weighty, they are like guarding a bright pearl. If one violates them...
One who is like a vessel already cracked is a person on the periphery of the Buddha-dharma. "Unbroken" means they maintain the thirteen [saṃghāvaśeṣa] precepts without any breach.
"Uncracked" refers to the *pāyattika* (pāyantika) offenses and so forth; if one commits such violations, it is like a vessel with holes and leaks, incapable of receiving the Way.
"Unmixed" means maintaining the *dhyāna-samvara* (meditative restraint); although one maintains the *vinaya-samvara* (disciplinary restraint), one still dwells upon thoughts of breaking the precepts.
It is called "mixed concentration" (*miśra-samādhi*) because it maintains the mind such that desires and discursive thoughts do not arise. A great sutra states:

"Idle chatter, wall-whistling sounds, and men and women pursuing one another all defile the pure precepts. "Following the Path" means to accord with the principle of the Truths (*satya*), thereby being able to destroy the delusions of views (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*).
"Non-attachment" means that having seen the Truth and become a sage, one has nothing to do with the delusions of cultivation (*bhāvanā-kleśa*).

Attachment to these two refers to the observance of the precepts according to ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*). The "precepts praised by wisdom" and the "precepts of mastery" refer to the Bodhisattva’s transformation of others;
being praised by the Buddha, one attains sovereignty within the world—this concerns the observance of the precepts according to conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).
When the two sets of precepts are fully endowed with meditative concentration (*samādhi*), they correspond to the *Śūraṅgama-samādhi*, wherein neither arising nor ceasing occurs.
Through meditative concentration, they manifest various modes of conduct (*īryāpatha*) and display the forms of the ten dharma realms to guide and benefit sentient beings;
yet because their movements and activities are spontaneously and eternally tranquil, this is called the "precept of following concentration.

While the various precepts and disciplines mentioned previously are termed "incomplete" because they involve restraint, this is called "complete" because there is no precept that is not fully prepared. It employs the wisdom of the Middle Way to pervade all.
Because one enters into all phenomena, it is called "endowment"; this is the precept of upholding the ultimate truth of the Middle Way.

Next, the stages and positions are elucidated: by inferring the meaning according to the various teaching gates expounded throughout the Buddha’s single transformation, the four teachings—namely, the *Āgama* (Tripitaka), the Shared, the Distinct, and the Perfect—are fully clarified, as the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* cites Kātyāyanīputra’s explanation of the limits of the six perfections, beginning with the precept of ethical discipline (*śīla*).
Videha is the fulfillment of *dāna* (generosity); King Māndhātṛ’s truthfulness is the fulfillment of *śīla* (ethical discipline);

the Immortal Seer Kāli’s heart remaining unmoved while being cut by King Kaliṅga is the fulfillment of *kṣānti* (patience); the Great Giver’s draining of the ocean is the fulfillment of *vīrya* (vigorous effort);

the Śāri bird’s nest is the fulfillment of *dhyāna* (meditative concentration); and Minister Gopaka’s division of the land to settle the dispute is the fulfillment of *samatājñāna* (equalizing wisdom).

This refers exclusively to Bodhisattvas. If one follows the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*, there are Bodhisattvas who resolve their minds in a way that accords with *sarvajñatā* (all-knowledge), which pertains to Bodhisattvas in general.
There are also those who resolve their minds to sport with supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*) and purify Buddha-fields;

yet, as seen in the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra*, there are those who attain inconceivable liberation (*acintya-vimokṣa*), manifest transformations, and ascend the seat, only to be subsequently humbled and rebuked—this refers to a specific category.

Bodhisattvas also have four types: the Bodhisattva who, upon generating the mind of enlightenment (*bodhicitta*), immediately sits at the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), attains perfect awakening (*samyaksambodhi*), turns the wheel of Dharma (*dharmacakra-pravartana*), and delivers sentient beings;
this is the perfected Bodhisattva. Among these four types of Bodhisattvas, the depths and shallowness of their stages and positions will now be explained.

First, regarding the three baskets (*tripiṭaka*), they primarily concern the Śrāvakas of the Hīnayāna. There are seven worthies (*saptakalyāṇapudgala*) and seven sages (*saptāryapudgala*). Among the external ordinary beings (*bāhyapṛthagjana*), there are three [stages], and among the internal ordinary beings (*adhyātmapṛthagjana*), there are five.

The stages are as follows: first, the two types of *sthāpanā* (stabilizing the mind); second, the four *smṛtyupasthānas* of specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*); third, the three *smṛtyupasthānas* of general characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*). Next, one enters the stage of the ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*), where there are four roots of merit (*kuśalamūla*):
fourth, the stage of Heat (*uṣmagata*); fifth, the stage of Summits (*mūrdhan*); sixth, the stage of Patience (*kṣānti*); and seventh, the stage of the Supreme Worldly Dharma (*laukikāgradharma*).

Beyond this, one enters the stage of the noble ones (*ārya*), consisting of: first, the follower by faith (*śraddhānusārin*); second, the follower by dharma (*dharmānusārin*); third, the one liberated through faith (*śraddhādhimukta*); fourth, the one who has attained vision (*dṛṣṭiprāpta*); and fifth, the one who has realized through the body (*kāyasākṣin*).

The Śrāvaka stages consist of those liberated at six times and those liberated at non-specific times. For a Bodhisattva, regardless of their stage, they do not sever the afflictions but only cultivate the six perfections;
however, when discussing their sequential stages, one may only gauge their depth by comparing them to the Small Vehicle (Hīnayāna).
From the initial generation of the mind of enlightenment, they give rise to compassion and vows, and observe the Four Noble Truths through the Path.

Taking the Truths as the initial gateway, he single-mindedly cultivated the six perfections: through *dāna* (generosity), he broke the bodies of hungry ghosts; through *kṣānti* (patience), he rescued those in the hells;
through *vīrya* (diligence), he delivered the animals; through *dhyāna* (meditation), he uprooted the asuras; and through *prajñā* (wisdom), he illuminated the celestial hosts among humans.

From the time of the first Śākya [Buddha] until Kṛkin and Śikhin, this is called the first *asaṃkhyeya-kalpa* (incalculable eon). During this period, he attained five kinds of merit: first, not being born in the three evil realms; second, ... [text continues].
1. Not being born in a border region; 2. Having all sense faculties complete; 3. Not receiving a female body; 4. Constantly knowing past lives; and 5.

Knowing for oneself whether one will become a Buddha or not—this stage corresponds to the positions of the five *sthāpanās* and the specific and general applications of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*).

From Śikhin to Dīpaṃkara is called the second *asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*; at that time, although one knows for oneself that one will become a Buddha, [the aforementioned five qualities are still not fully perfected].
He does not speak of it with his mouth; he abides in the stage of the "Heat" (*uṣmagata*) within the level of the Dharma-nature.

Since he possesses faith that has realized the Dharma, he certainly knows he will become a Buddha, yet because his mind in practicing the six perfections is not yet clear, he does not speak of it to others.

From the time of Dīpaṃkara until Vipaśyin, when the three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas* are fulfilled, at that moment he clearly knows within his own heart that he will become a Buddha, though he does not speak of it with his mouth.

From the moment he utters these words, he is reckoned to be within the stage of the Dharma at the Summit (*mūrdhan*), where he practices the six perfections and clearly understands the Four Noble Truths;

because it is like ascending a mountain peak and seeing clearly in all four directions, he speaks to others. If he has passed through three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas* and planted the karma for the thirty-two marks, he is reckoned to be in the stage of Lower Patience (*adhimātra-ksānti*);
if he sits at the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), he is in the stage of Higher Patience (*adhimātra-ksānti*).
In the subsequent single moment, entering the true [path] through thirty-four moments of mind, one severs the fetters and attains *sambodhi*, thereby becoming a Buddha.
In the Shared Teaching (*pāryāya-yāna*), the Bodhisattva follows the ten stages common to the Three Vehicles: first, the Stage of Dry Wisdom (*śuṣka-vipaśyanā-bhūmi*).

While the names of the phenomenal characteristics are identical to those in the Tripiṭaka, the mental state of contemplative practice differs; one perceives the aggregates, elements, and sense bases as being like illusions and transformations, collectively destroying both views and craving.

The eight inversions are termed the foundations of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna) regarding body, mind, feeling, and phenomena; abiding likewise within this contemplation, one cultivates right effort, the faculties, the powers, the factors of enlightenment, and the path.

Although one has not yet attained the stage of "Heat" (ūṣmagata), because the wisdom of the general characteristics—which resembles the water of principle—is profound and sharp, it is called the Stage of Dry Wisdom (śuklavipaśyanā-bhūmi). Second, the Stage of Nature (gotra-bhūmi): having transcended the Stage of Dry Wisdom, one attains "Heat."

Regarding the "Stage of Nature" (*dharmatā-bhūmi*): when one has already been able to progress through the initial, middle, and final stages of the mind, entering the *mūrdhan* (Summits) and even reaching the *laukikāgra-dharma* (Supreme Mundane Dharmas), these are all called the Stage of Nature.

Because one attains the water of the untainted nature (*anāsrava-dharmatā*), it is termed the "Stage of Nature. Regarding the "Eight Persons' Stages" (*aṣṭapudgala-bhūmi*): this refers to the three vehicles’ practitioners of faith (*śraddhānusārin*) and practitioners of dharma (*dharmānusārin*).

Their essence consists of the provisional seeing that triggers the realization of the truth (*satyābhisamaya*) and the severance of delusions within the *ānantarya-samādhi* (Uninterrupted Samādhi). There are eight such stages.
The stage of the Eight Persons (*aṣṭamaka-bhūmi*) is so named because it possesses patience and wisdom, yet lacks one part [of full realization].

The stage of the Four Views (*darśana-bhūmi*) refers to the common vision of the three vehicles regarding the ultimate principle of the four truths of non-arising; they equally sever the delusions of view, exhausting all eighty-eight latent proclivities (*anuśaya*).

The stage of Thinness (*tanu-bhūmi*) means that while the substance of craving remains, the provisional has given way to the real, as one severs the afflictions of the desire realm and realizes the sixth liberation.

Sixth, the stage of freedom from desire (*vītarāgabhūmi*): because those of the three vehicles realize that the essence of craving for the realm of form and formlessness is itself the truth, they sever the five lower fetters (*pañca avarabhāgīyāni saṃyojanāni*)—namely, the view of a self-body (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), attachment to precepts and rituals (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*), doubt (*vicikitsā*), greed (*rāga*), and hatred (*dveṣa*). Therefore, it is called the stage of freedom from desire. Seventh, the stage of having already accomplished what was to be done (*kṛtāvibhūmi*):

those of the three vehicles realize that the essence of craving for the realms of form and formlessness is itself the truth; they give rise to untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*) and sever the five [higher fetters].

The Stage of Having Accomplished What Was to Be Done (*kṛtāvibhūmi*) is so called because one has exhausted the seventy-two afflictions of the upper realms—the fetters of the higher parts (*ūrdhvabhāgīya-saṃyojana*), restlessness (*auddhatya*), pride (*māna*), ignorance (*avidyā*), attachment to the realm of form (*rūparāga*), and attachment to the formless realm (*ārūpyarāga*)—and has brought to completion all matters concerning the delusions of the three realms. The Eighth, the Stage of the Pratyekabuddha (*pratyekabuddhabhūmi*), refers to the Pratyekabuddhas who have given rise to true, untainted merit and power;
their great capacity enables them to eliminate residual habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*). The Ninth, the Stage of the Bodhisattva (*bodhisattvabhūmi*), refers to those who enter from emptiness...
Borrowing the path to contemplate the two streams and deeply observing the two truths, one advances to sever habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*).

When both form and mind are devoid of cognition, one attains the Dharma-eye and the knowledge of the modes of the Path (*mārgajñatā*), sporting with supernatural powers (*abhijñā*) and purifying Buddha-lands to bring sentient beings to maturity.

By training in the ten powers (*bala*) and four fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*) of a Buddha, one brings the habitual tendencies to their end. As for the ten Buddha-stages (*daśa-bhūmi*), they consist of the power of great merit.
Relying on wisdom, through the wisdom of a single thought-moment in resonance, one contemplates the ultimate truth;

even habitual tendencies are exhausted without remainder, like a kalpa-fire consuming wood until not even ash or charcoal remains. Like a fragrant elephant crossing a river to its very bottom, although the names "Buddha" and "Bodhisattva" differ from those of the Two Vehicles, they all universally contemplate non-arising;
their realization of the essence of dharmas is identical as they are all Arhats who have returned to the cessation of ashes.

The single stage of fruition is called "penetration. In the Separate Teaching (*biejiao*), there are fifty-two stages: first, the outer ordinary person (*wailun fanfu*) consists of the ten levels of faith:
(1) faith, (2) mindfulness, (3) progress, (4) wisdom, (5) concentration, (6) non-retrogression, (7) dedication, (8) protection of the Dharma, (9) precepts, and (10) vows.

Second, the inner ordinary person (*neilun fanfu*) consists of the nature of the seeds of practice (*xizhongxing*), which comprises the ten abodes: (1) the arousal of the mind (*faxin*), (2) subduing [the afflictions]... [and so forth].

The ten stages are: first, the stage of dry wisdom; second, the stage of superior understanding; third, the stage of the nature-seed; fourth, the stage of practice through understanding; fifth, the stage of noble birth; sixth, the stage of perfection in skillful means;

seventh, the stage of the right mind; eighth, the stage of non-retrogression; ninth, the stage of the youthful prince; tenth, the stage of the Dharma-son; and eleventh, the stage of consecration. These thirty minds are all termed the stage of practice through understanding (*adhimukti-caryā-bhūmi*); they are all internal ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) and are collectively termed the stage of the nature-ground (*prakṛti-bhūmi*). Third is the stage of the nature-seed (*gotra-bhūmi*), which consists of the ten practices: first, the practice of joy; second, [the practice of virtue]; third, [the practice of tolerance]; fourth, [the practice of vigor]; fifth, [the practice of meditation]; sixth, [the practice of wisdom]; seventh, [the practice of skillful means]; eighth, [the practice of vows]; ninth, [the practice of power]; and tenth, [the practice of knowledge]. First is the practice of joy (*pramuditā-caryā*); second... [and so on].
1. Beneficial Conduct; 2. Freedom from Enmity and Resentment; 3. Exhaustlessness; 4. Freedom from Delusion and Confusion; 5. Skillful Vision; 6. Non-attachment; 7. Veneration; 8.
Wholesome Dharmas; 9. Reality; 10. The Fourth Nature of the Path. The Ten Dedications (*pariṇāmanā*): 1.
Saving and Protecting All Sentient Beings while Remaining Free from the Notion of Sentient Beings; 2. The Indestructible; 3. Equalizing with All Buddhas; 4. [The Dedication of] ... [text fragment].
1. Pervasively reaching all places; 2. The inexhaustible treasury of five meritorious qualities; 3. Accordance with all firm and equal roots of goodness; 4.
Accordance with the impartial contemplation of all sentient beings; 5. The characteristic of *tathatā* (suchness); 6. Liberation that is unbound and unattached; 7.
The immeasurable realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*); 8. The fifth noble lineage; 9. The ten stages (*bhūmi*), beginning with the first, the Joyful (*pramuditā*).

The second is Vimalā (Stainless), the third Trayodaśī (Thirteen), the fourth Arciṣmatī (Radiant), the fifth Sudurjayā (Difficult to Conquer), the sixth Abhimukhī (Manifest), the seventh Dūraṅgamā (Far-Reaching), the eighth Acalā (Immovable), the ninth Sādhumatī (Excellent Intelligence), and the tenth Dharmameghā (Cloud of Dharma). The sixth stage, the Ground of Equal Enlightenment, is called the Bodhisattva of the Vajra-Mind;

it is also named the Stainless Ground (*vimalā-bhūmi*), the pinnacle of the training for the assembly of those who approach ultimate holiness. The seventh is the Ground of Wondrous Enlightenment, which is the final consummation.

Upon the ultimate attainment of the fruit of Buddha-bodhi, one clearly perceives the nature; this is called wondrous enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*). Regarding the two natures—the nature-inherent (*prakṛti*) and the nature-accustomed (*vāsanā*):

if distinguished by their stages, the nature-accustomed precedes and the nature-inherent follows; however, if discussed according to their activity, the nature-inherent and the nature-accustomed are simultaneous. Thus, their sequence is not fixed.
Since activity arises from the essence, the nature-seed is explained first and the nature-accustomed seed is explained afterward; one seeks the essence by means of its activity.

Regarding the sequence of essence (*tattva*), prior practice (*pūrva-abhyāsa*), subsequent nature (*paścāt-prakṛti*), and the two paths of teaching (*deśanā-mārga*) and realization (*adhigama-mārga*):

if discussed according to their respective stages, the path of teaching comes first and the path of realization follows; however, if discussed according to actual practice, realization and teaching are simultaneous, and thus the sequence is not fixed.

In terms of the arising of function (*vṛtti*) from essence, realization precedes teaching; in terms of seeking the essence through function, teaching precedes realization. This is based on the perspective of understanding (*adhimukti*) and practice (*caryā*).
Within this, there are further four types: first, the stage of practice through understanding (*adhimukti-caryā*); second, the generation of the resolve (*cittotpāda*);

third, dedication (*pariṇāmanā*); and fourth, the lineage of the path (*mārga-jāti*). It is called the stage of practice through understanding because one understands and diligently practices the supramundane path.

It is called the generation of the resolve because one conceives the intention and seeks toward great enlightenment (*mahābodhi*). It is called dedication because one directs one's already cultivated wholesome dharmas toward enlightenment.
Because it is established as the Path within its own stage, it is called the "Path" (*mārga*); because it can produce the subsequent fruit of Buddhahood, it is called the "Seed" (*gotra*).

The nature of the *śikṣā-gotra* (cultivated seed-nature) can produce the *saṃbhoga-buddha*, and the nature of the *prakṛti-gotra* (innate seed-nature) can produce the *dharma-buddha*. [The term] formerly translated as "Prince Dharmatāla" refers to the regression from the sixth mind; that is to say, the sixth mind of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*).

Regarding the question of why it is called the "sixth mind of the ten stages," it is said: [it is so called because... (Note: The final sentence fragment regarding the "sixth mind of the ten stages" appears to be an editorial or commentarial note appended to the source text.)

The nature of the "ground-nature" (bhūmi-prakṛti) is defined by its unchanging character. How then can one regress to become a follower of the Two Vehicles? This is like a single response: the nature is such that one does not become an icchantika;
it does not preclude regressing from the Great Vehicle toward the Small, yet ultimately this remains difficult to reconcile.

Master Zhizhe of Zhi-guan says that among the ten stages of faith, it is only during the first six minds that regression occurs. This is comparable to the explanations of the *Vyākhyāyukti* master and the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā*.
The masters all provide this interpretation: these are merely the six stages among the ten minds of faith and practice; from the seventh mind upward, one is forever separated from the two vehicles.

At that time, even if one were to preach the sutra for the sake of benefit, though there might be no lack of slight leakage, the intention to save sentient beings does not lose its constancy, and thus one possesses the name of a Bodhisattva.
Because the *Yuanjiao* (Perfect Teaching) clarifies the distinctness of the stages, there are fifty-two positions.
The sequential cultivation of practice differs from the perfect cultivation of the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*), which involves the single mind encompassing all practices.
Within the five grades of the outer ordinary stage (*wailan wu pinwei*), first is the mind of sympathetic joy (*suixi xin*):

if a person has planted deep roots in the past, or encounters a virtuous friend (*shanzhishi*), or hears the wondrous principle through the scriptures—that one dharma is all dharmas and all dharmas are one dharma.
The Dharma is neither one nor all; it arises from the inconceivable and gives rise to perfect faith and understanding.

One should believe that within a single mind, the ten dharma realms are fully contained, just as a great thousand-fold world-system scripture is contained within a single mote of dust. Desiring to open this mind, one practices the perfect conduct.
Perfect conduct means that a single practice encompasses all practices; briefly stated, these are ten, namely: realizing the equality of a single thought-moment.
Fully endowed with inconceivable compassion for oneself and all others, even amidst affliction and dullness;

furthermore, knowing that this mind is eternally quiescent and eternally illuminating, one uses this mind of quiescence and illumination to shatter all phenomena as being simultaneously empty, provisional, and the Middle Way.

Moreover, recognizing that within the single mind all minds—whether unobstructed or obstructed—are contained, one can fully perfect the factors of enlightenment within this very mind and advance toward Bodhi.
Furthermore, Daoxuan explained that this mind involves the methods of the primary and auxiliary practices; it recognizes both one's own mind and the minds of ordinary beings and sages.

Moreover, by settling the mind so that it is immovable—neither falling away, nor regressing, nor dispersing—one recognizes the immeasurable merits of the One Mind without giving rise to defiled attachment.
When the ten minds are perfected, every thought-moment of the mind is in complete accord with all the *pāramitās*.

Second, regarding those who recite and chant: when perfect faith first arises, one must nurture the arising of wholesome roots. If one becomes involved in worldly affairs and distractions, the sprouts of the Path will be broken.
One may only cultivate internal contemplation; externally, one should recite and chant the Mahāyāna, for hearing the Dharma provides the power to assist contemplation.
When the internal and external support one another, perfect faith becomes increasingly clear, and the ten mental states become as firm as the sun’s light illuminating all varieties of phenomena.

Furthermore, when one preaches the Dharma, internal contemplation becomes increasingly firm and external conditions provide further support; as a perfect understanding dwells within the heart and great vows stir the mind, one preaches the Dharma even more so, expounding it according to reality.
One answers solely with the Mahāyāna teachings, and even if expedient means are employed, they ultimately lead others to realize the Great Vehicle.
As the preaching of the Dharma becomes pure, wisdom becomes pure; this preaching that guides and enlightens is [the path].
That former person attained the Way entirely through the power of transformation from causes and conditions, which returned to himself; thus the ten minds were transformed into threefold clarity.

Fourth, the concurrent practice of the six pāramitās: whereas previously one was occupied with maturely contemplating the mind and had not yet had leisure to engage with phenomena, now that right contemplation is somewhat clear, one may concurrently benefit others by the side.
One can take even a small gift and make it equal to empty space, causing all dharmas to incline toward *dāna* (generosity).

In the practice of *dāna* (giving), although the phenomenal characteristics of the *dharmadhātu* are few, the movement of the mind is exceedingly vast. Contemplation (*prajñā*) is the primary practice, while conduct (*caryā*) is secondary;

thus it is said that this practice is "concurrent with active deeds. Merit from active deeds supports principle, and as the ten mental states flourish even more, the five correct practices and the six perfections (*ṣaṭpāramitā*) become mature through complete contemplation.
As phenomena and principle are about to merge, phenomena do not obstruct principle, and principle does not separate from phenomena; one fully accomplishes the six practices.

Having mastered and thoroughly penetrated the two wisdoms of the provisional and the real, one ensures that all activities for livelihood and production do not contradict the true aspect (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*).
One fully explains the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, and through right contemplation, the power and function of this practice become as fierce and brilliant as adding fuel to a fire.
This is the first stage of the inner ordinary person: the ten stages of faith, wherein one hears the perfect teaching, attains perfect faith, and cultivates perfect practice with goodness.
Skillfully augmenting [the practice] fivefold, one deeply clarifies this through which the perfect practice attains entry into the stage of perfection.

Skillfully cultivating the equal Dharma-realm, one enters the mind of faith; skillfully cultivating compassion, one enters the mind of mindfulness; skillfully cultivating stillness and illumination, one enters the mind of diligence;
skillfully cultivating the breaking of dharmas, one enters the mind of wisdom; skillfully cultivating penetration and obstruction, one enters the mind of concentration.

Skillfully cultivating the factors of the path leads to entry into the mind of non-retrogression; skillfully cultivating the primary and auxiliary practices leads to entry into the mind of dedication;

skillfully cultivating the mundane and the sacred leads to entry into the mind of protecting the Dharma; skillfully cultivating immovability leads to entry into the mind of precepts; skillfully cultivating non-attachment leads to entry into the mind of vows.
These are called the ten stages of faith (*śraddhā*) of the Iron Wheel in the Perfect Teaching (*yāna*), representing the sixth stage of semblance-understanding in the Perfect Teaching.

This is the purity of the faculties (*indriya-viśuddhi*). Prior to the second stage of the noble ones (*ārya-bhūmi*), it clarifies the true-middle wisdom (*bhūtatathatā-madhyama-jñāna*) of the ten abodes (*daśa-vihāra*).

When the first dwelling, the Dwelling of Initial Resolve (*prathama-cittotpāda-vihāra*), arises, three kinds of mind arise: first, the arising of the mind of good as the *pratyaya-hetu* (conditioning cause);

second, the arising of the mind of wisdom as the *pariniṣpanna-hetu* (fulfilling cause); and third, the arising of the mind of principle as the *bīja-hetu* (causal seed). These are precisely the threefold development of the excellence of object, wisdom, and practice; specifically, the mind of the conditioning cause.

The arousal [of the mind] is precisely abiding in the *śūraṅgama-samādhi*, the inconceivable liberation; the arousal of the *pariniṣpanna-hetu* (fulfillment cause) mind is precisely the ultimate emptiness of *mahāprajñā*;
and the arousal of the *samyag-hetu* (correct cause) mind is precisely abiding within the *dharmakāya* of the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*), the Middle Way, and the primary truth (*paramārtha-satya*).
As the *Avataṃsaka* states: "All the merits possessed by a Bodhisattva in the first stage..."

The virtues of the Buddhas of the three periods of time cannot be fully extolled; at the very moment of first generating the resolve for enlightenment (*prathama-cittotpāda*), one attains perfect awakening and thoroughly realizes the true nature of all phenomena.
All hearing of the Dharma is not through another's guidance but is self-realized. As the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* states:

"To know that all phenomena are [empty] is to sit upon the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*)," and it is also the entry into the gate of non-duality (*advaya-dvāra*). The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* states: "From the first generation of the resolve..."
The mind itself sits upon the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa), turns the wheel of Dharma, and delivers sentient beings, becoming like a Buddha.

The letter "A" gate signifies that all phenomena are fundamentally unarisen. Third, the clarification of the ten practices (*daśacaryā*) refers to the inconceivable true illumination of the ultimate reality (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) following the ten abodes (*daśavihāra*).
It further realizes ten successive stages of wisdom and severance, thereby destroying the ten grades of ignorance (*avidyā*). This constitutes the first practice.
All conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) progress moment by moment, flowing into the ocean of the equal Dharma-realm;
all the *pāramitās* grow spontaneously, benefiting oneself and others, becoming equal to space. This is the fortieth dedication:
following the ten practices (*daśa-caryā*), the path of effortless spontaneity (*anābhoga-mārga*) unfolds, and inconceivable true illumination develops moment by moment throughout all things.
The practice of the Dharma-realm vow naturally harmonizes principle and phenomena, returning them into the ocean of the equal Dharma-realm;
by further realizing the ten stages of wisdom and severing the ten grades of ignorance, it is called "dedication" (*pariṇāmanā*).
The fifth stage, the tenth ground (*bhūmi*), is the untainted true illumination that enters the path of non-effort (*anābhoga-mārga*); like the great earth, it is able to give birth to all things.

The Buddha-dharma involves bearing the burden of sentient beings throughout the Dharma-realm, universally entering the stages of the Buddhas of the three periods of time, and further realizing the tenfold wisdom and abandonment to shatter the ten grades of ignorance.
Regarding the sixth stage, Equal Enlightenment (Samantaprabhā-bhūmi): through contemplation, one penetrates to the very source and limit of beginningless ignorance;
wisdom is perfected and becomes ultimately pure, as one abandons the final, most subtle ignorance that reaches the very root of existence.
To ascend to the summit of the Middle Way and part from the parents of ignorance is called "that which has something to be severed"; such a person is termed a "Superior Person" (uttama-puruṣa).

As for the seventh stage, the Stage of Wondrous Enlightenment (samyak-saṃbodhi), because it is ultimate liberation and the unsurpassed Buddha-wisdom, it is said that "there is nothing further to be severed";
such a person is termed an "Unsurpassed Person" (anuttara-puruṣa). This is precisely the Three Virtues (triguṇa), neither vertical nor horizontal, neither parallel nor...

It is distinct from the ultimate mind at the end of life and the Great Nirvana. All great principles, great vows, great adornments, great wisdom, great severance, great universal knowledge, the Great Way, great function, great provisional and real [teachings], great benefit, and great non-abiding—this is the fulfillment of the Ten Contemplations as the Perfect Vehicle.
It culminates in the Buddha; beyond this, there is no word to be spoken. Lu.
The character "she" (捨, *pra*) signifies purity; when it is complete, all things are complete. Master Nanyue said: "The forty-two letter-gates are the secret language of the Buddha;
why should they not symbolize the forty-two stages? Many students cling to the *Vyākhyāyukti* (Shelun) because it lacks this interpretation, and thus harbor many doubts and do not accept it.
Yet, while the original treatise consists of one thousand fascicles, Master Kumārajīva condensed it ninefold—how could he have omitted such a point?"
There can certainly be no such interpretation; one must surely realize this through profound resonance. Why? For the Sūtra says:

"From the first letter *a* to the last letter *ḍa*, the forty-one letters in between constitute the 'letter-gate' (*akṣaramukha*) that possesses the merit of all letters. The *Avataṃsaka* states: "From the first stage, one is fully endowed with the merits of all stages.
This meaning is identical to the *a*-letter gate, wherein all phenomena are fundamentally unarisen. How could this possibly be...?

It is not that the attainment of the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharmakṣānti*) by those in the first stage (*prathama-bhūmi*) of the Perfect Teaching (*pariniṣpanna-yāna*) surpasses what can be expressed beyond the letter *ḍa*; how could it be otherwise?
In the "Chapter on the Vast Vehicle" (*Guangsheng pin*), after it is concluded that all phenomena are the Mahāyāna, the forty-two letter-gates (*dvātriṃśad-akṣara-mukha*) are then expounded;
how could this not mean that the Bodhisattvas of the Perfect Teaching attain the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena from the very moment they first resolve their minds?
"Being endowed with all dharmas and reaching the stage of supreme enlightenment, one exhausts the depths of all dharmas"—this meaning is extremely clear regarding the Perfect Stage (*yuanwei*).
Next, in the "Chapter on Progression," the ten stages of the Separate Teaching (*biejiao*) are clarified, followed by the ten stages common to the Three Vehicles;
the textual evidence for these hierarchical positions of the three teachings is manifest therein.

○ Second, regarding the definition of the essence [of the precepts]: first, the non-active (avijñapti) is clarified; next, the two virtues of cessation and cultivation are clarified. First, concerning the essence of the precept: it is simply that which does not arise.

Once arisen, it is an unconditioned, non-active, derivative matter (rūpa). The sūtras and śāstras discuss this alternately, debating its existence or non-existence. One school says: "There is no such thing as non-active matter;
sentient beings are formed by the provisional conjunction of mind and matter. Good and evil fundamentally originate from the mind."
It should not be held that there exists a separate, stubborn entity [apart from the mind]. Whether it be stubbornly good or stubbornly evil, both refer to the mind.

The vow not to commit evil is itself called "receiving the precepts. The *Yingluo jing* states: "The precepts of all sages and ordinary beings alike take the mind as their essence; because the mind is inexhaustible, the precepts are also inexhaustible.
Some say that the verbal teaching is the essence of the precepts, while others say that ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) is the essence of the precepts. Or...

It is said: "May it be that the essence of the precepts (śīla-svabhāva) is without distinction or activity; the noble practice of the Great Sūtra analyzes impermanence through contemplation, while the *Aśoka-rāja-vyākaraṇa* analyzes the objective realm.
These clarify only matter and mind, and do not speak of non-informative action (avijñapti). The teaching of the five aggregates is common to both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna;
there is only one aggregate of matter and four aggregates of mind. The Hīnayāna was introduced for those of lesser faculties, fearing they might treat [the Dharma] with contempt."
Cause and effect are spoken of as provisional; it is the mind that creates good and evil. A distinct dharma called "unmanifest" (*avijñapti*) arises separately, which draws forth retribution.
Good dharmas must be practiced and evil dharmas must be ceased. When one practices [the former], there are two powers; how can one not be careful?

These are skillful means and provisional designations suited to the occasion. It is simply like the Master of the Treatise [Vasubandhu] attaining the four fruits in a single lifetime; such excellence of the Dharma is indeed distinct.

How could the dharmas of ordinary beings, based on this, be considered real? If there were distinct, insentient wholesome factors within the causal stage that together constitute the cause for Buddhahood, and if there were likewise distinct wholesome factors in the stage of Buddhahood that together constitute the fruit of Buddhahood, one should know that mind alone constitutes cause and effect, with no other dharma existing apart from it.
Second, all Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna sūtras and śāstras contain the doctrine of "unmanifest" (avijñapti), and all of these are real.
What is this dharma? It is the power of the mind, which is vast and immense, capable of producing all manner of dharmas and drawing forth their karmic retributions.

The Śrāvaka-vehicle clarifies that there is this single wholesome faculty capable of establishing the Buddha-dharma. Whether one receives and generates it by relying on a teacher for as long as one lives, or whether it arises separately based on meditative concentration (*samādhi*) or the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipākṣika-dharma*), it is all due to the superior function of the mental power that brings about such inspiration and realization—so states the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya*.

There is a work titled *Wu zuopin* (The Collection of Non-Works) which states that this is neither an aggregate of matter (*rūpa*) nor an aggregate of mind (*citta*). The Vinaya Master uses this meaning as his basis for explanation.

According to the *Abhidharma* (Vibhāṣā) school, the precept (*śīla*) is an aggregate of matter; it is an unmanifested form (*avijñapti-rūpa*) and is also called "non-informative" (*avijñapti*), yet it is not a form that is perceptible to the eye.
As for the precept elucidated in the Mahayana, it is a dharma of matter. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* asks: "Since the precept is a dharma of matter, it may be discussed [as such]."

"How many thoughts are mental concomitants (*caitta*)? Why do you say 'how many'?"—observing the intent of the *Abhidharma-kośa*, [the author] takes precepts (*śīla*) to be form (*rūpa*) and thus asks about this meaning of "concomitant" (*saṃkhyā*).
How does the Mahāyāna employ this meaning of "concomitant"? The explanation says:

if one employs it as being neither form nor mind, then it is again the same as the *Tattvasiddhi* (Satyasiddhi-śāstra) and thus remains within the Small Vehicle (*Hīnayāna*). Now, when we speak of the "school of numbers" (*saṃkhyā-vāda*), it is simply that these are numbers of form.
The Mahāyāna is the form (rūpa) of the Mahāyāna; what concern does this have with the Abhidharma masters? The *Śāstra on the Middle Way* states:

"Though their words may be the same, their minds differ. Now, the Mahāyāna clarifies that the precepts are an aggregate of form (rūpa-skandha). The aspiration of the Mahāyāna aims at the ultimate fruit; relying on a teacher for a single reception [of the vows], it extends far to Bodhi.
In accordance with meditative concentration and the Path, one vows to cultivate all virtues and vows to deliver all sentient beings. Furthermore—
By the power of this mind, one specifically generates the wholesome discipline (*śīla*) as an object of focus for the practitioner, thereby bringing all evils to rest.

The *Upāsaka-śīla-sūtra* states: "Just as when there is a face and a mirror, a reflection appears; so too, because of the 'informative' (*vijñapti*) action, there arises the 'non-informative' (*avijñapti') [action].

The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, in its explanation of the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīla-pāramitā*), says: "Sin and non-sin are unapprehendable; one is fully endowed with ethical discipline (*śīla*)."

This is the true essence of the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīla-pāramitā*). Furthermore, why is it called "ethical discipline"? Because when the mind gives rise to verbal expression, one vows from this moment forth to cease the unwholesome states of body and speech;

this is what is termed "ethical discipline. Since there is both that which is able to maintain [the precepts] and that which is maintained, there exists a distinct phenomenon, namely "unmanifest action" (*avijñapti*).
The *Bodhisattvabhūmi*, in the chapter on Ethical Discipline, states: "If one violates the latter four grave offenses with a weak or inferior state of mind..."

If one commits a transgression through the loss of restraint or the superior mind (*adhi-citta*), then one loses the restraint; however, if one does not abandon the vow for enlightenment, even committing a transgression through the non-superior mind, one does not lose the restraint.
If there were no such thing as non-manifest action (*avijñapti*) at all, how could it be said that the *Brahmajāla Sūtra*—the fundamental text of the Mahāyāna teaching—is lost?
As the subsequent passage states: "Even if one does not see auspicious signs before the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas..."

Receiving [the precepts] is not called "attaining the precepts. Furthermore, it is said that if one has the seven obstacles (*saptāvaraṇa*), even if one generates the aspiration to receive them, it is not called attaining the precepts.
If the mind alone were the precept, such that generating the aspiration itself constituted the precept, why would it be said that one does not attain them? A great sutra states:

"A cause that is not distinct from form does not produce an effect that is distinct from form. Moreover, although there is no visible form within the recollection of the precepts (*śīlānusmṛti*), [it is still the precept].
Yet it can be guarded and maintained; even without physical contact, through the skillful cultivation of means, one may bring it to fulfillment.
Furthermore, just as with a sword, lye, feet, or a bridge, if the mind itself were the precept, why rely on words?

Since there is no form or color and no physical contact, we know that there exists separately the "unmanifest" (*avijñapti*) which is able to sustain the mind that intends to keep the precepts, serving as the true precept and holy practice.

Among the kings of the world, it is not taught that one contemplates by analyzing the unconditioned (*avijñapti*); rather, to directly cite matter and mind is merely to provide a concise summary for ease of contemplation.
Nor does it say that there is no *avijñapti*. The Small Vehicle speaks of the four fruits [of the path], while the Great Vehicle opens this up as a provisional teaching (*upāya-dharma*).
Regarding the dharmas of ordinary beings, Saṃghavarman clarified that they do not exist; yet, there has not yet been a Mahāyāna sūtra that explicitly opens up the existence of the unconditioned.

To act with such skillful means (*upāya*) is also inherently wholesome; because it is the cause for attaining Buddhahood, it does not obstruct itself. This is analogous to the case where that which is conditionally wholesome is not ultimately wholesome, as its very nature is the cause of that [unwholesomeness].
Regarding these two interpretations, there has long been debate among the ancients: if one says "it is non-existent," it accords perfectly with reason, yet it is difficult to reconcile with the text;
if one says "it exists," it is difficult to establish logically, yet it is extremely convenient in terms of the text. Since both positions have their grounds...
What, then, is it that accords with principle? Indeed, principle is neither "accordant" nor "non-accordant"; both accordance and non-accordance can be used to discuss the principles of the teachings.
If one says "it does not exist," this is accordant with principle; if one says "it exists," this is accordant with the teaching.
Principle is the reality (*tattva*), while the teaching is the skillful means (*upāya*). Although there is no gate of the teaching within reality, it nonetheless exists here in the present.

That which is employed is non-informative action (*avijñapti*). Next, it is explained that both the path-concomitant (*mārga-samprayukta*) and the restraint-concomitant (*dhyāna-samvara*) take non-informative action as their essence.

Regarding the "restraint-concomitant," because non-informative action is produced within the concentrated mind of meditative absorption (*samādhi*), it is free from all evil paths; thus, it is called "restraint-concomitant.

Regarding the "path-concomitant," because the non-informative action produced within the path of seeing the truths (*darśana-mārga*) coexists with the superior path of the mind, it is called "path-concomitant. This interpretation by Master Zhiguan is not necessarily definitive.

The unmanifest (avijñapti) produced by the Path of Seeing is the precept concomitant with the Path (*mārga-samvara*). This unmanifest is produced specifically within the mind of the Middle Way’s correct contemplation;

because it possesses the sense of preventing wrongdoing and ceasing evil, it is called "concomitant with the Path. As the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra* states: "First is the attainment of the Dharma-precept, second is the reception of the worldly teaching-precept.
When a Bodhisattva attains the Dharma-precept, this refers to the precept concomitant with the Path; upon attaining this precept, [one is established].

One who never commits evil because they do not follow the instructions of a teacher is said to have "attained" the Middle Way; this precept arises from within the mind, and thus it is called "attained.

Receiving the precepts of worldly instruction means that one only obtains them after the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* (the formal ritual of four motions); because this necessarily relies upon a teacher, it is called "received.
This distinction is stated for the sake of clarification; it refers to the precepts associated with meditative concentration (*samādhi-saṃvara*) and those common to the Path (*mārga-saṃvara*).
Regarding the inclusion of the *saṃvara-śīla* (precepts for gathering wholesome dharmas) within the meditative concentrations (*samādhi*) of the Mahāyāna path of both the Great and Small Vehicles:

some masters say that only the eight dhyāna-concentrations can give rise to the *avijñapti* (unmanifest karma), whereas the *kāmadhātu-samādhi* cannot give rise to the *avijñapti*; they claim that only through the provisional understanding of emptiness (*śūnyatā*) can the *avijñapti* be produced.
Others say that as long as one realizes this path of concentration, and is able to suppress the coarse categories [of afflictions], the *avijñapti* is accomplished and produced.
Prior to the establishment of the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) within the dhyāna of the desire realm, one is able to generate the precepts.
Next, regarding their arising and ceasing: initially, when one seeks to receive the essence of the bodhisattva vows through skillful means, they arise;
however, if one abandons the aspiration for enlightenment (*bodhicitta*) or commits the ten grave offenses due to predominant afflictions, their essence ceases. If these [conditions] do not exist...

Regarding the two conditions—attaining concentration (*samādhi*) and attaining the Path (*mārga*)—only upon reaching Buddhahood are the two precepts of concentration and the Path abandoned. Attaining concentration and attaining the Path serve as the causes.

In the first moment, concentration and the Path have not yet been conjoined with the precepts; the preceding mind serves as the cause. It is only in the second moment that the mind is conjoined with the precepts.
At that time, one emerges from concentration and the Path. This occurs at the very last moment, when the two [precepts] are simultaneously abandoned. Thus it is said: "Entering."

When entering meditative absorption (*samāpatti*) or the Path (*mārga*), the precept arises together with the mind; this is called its "arising. When emerging from absorption or the Path, the precept ceases together with the mind;

this is called its "cessation. Therefore, it is termed a "precept that arises with the mind" (*cittānuparivartin*). Regarding the third point: once it has been initiated, it is constantly present during both entry and emergence.

Subsequently, when one enters a superior absorption or a superior path, the precept receives its name according to that superior state. At that time, it is constantly arising, even when [the mind] regresses.
The three categories of precepts—concentration, the path, and the three baskets—are abandoned at the end of one’s life; for a bodhisattva, they are abandoned upon reaching enlightenment.

At that time, the precepts for gathering wholesome qualities and gathering sentient beings are likewise abandoned; they arise when one formally undertakes them and are abandoned when those two conditions cease.

Next, regarding the essence of the three clusters of precepts: *vinaya* (discipline) refers to the formal methods, rules, and regulations that lead the practitioner into the Way. It is also called *vinaya*.

"Railing" (埒) refers to a horse-racing track; just as it is used to train horses to be well-disciplined and straight, the *vinaya* is likewise used to discipline and straighten the practitioner so that they do not commit evil.
The Great Being’s vow does not exceed the cessation of evil and the promotion of good. If one does not move body or speech, this is the cessation of evil.
To prevent movement by means of the arising of the precepts (*śīla*)—such that there is no movement—is the *saṃvara-śīla* (restraint-precept). If one should move the body...

The mouth is that which gives rise to goodness; now, by initiating this precept, one prevents it from wavering. To encompass goodness and to encompass living beings is precisely what requires movement and engagement with affairs;
thus, it is opened into two aspects. To exert oneself toward all forms of goodness by means of the six perfections is called "encompassing wholesome dharmas" (*śīla-saṃgraha*);
to give rise to the mind that includes all beings by means of the four great vows is called "encompassing sentient beings. This is for the sake of others.
While actively transforming sentient beings below, one cultivates the myriad virtues to ascend toward the fruit of Buddhahood above.

Since the *vinaya* (precepts) primarily govern internal virtue while the "gathering of beings" (*sattvasaṃgraha*) governs external transformation, and the "gathering of good" (*kuśalasaṃgraha*) encompasses both the internal and the external, the three clusters of precepts (*trisaṃvara-śīla*) are established.

Next, we discuss the two virtues of cessation and cultivation: as the *Śata-śāstra* states, refraining from evil and not committing it is called "cessation" (*sthiti*), while faithfully accepting, practicing, and cultivating [the good] is called "cultivation" (*pravṛtti*).
This is termed "practice" (*caryā*). Although the Buddhist teachings are numerous, they are fully encompassed within practice and cessation.

"Commit no evil" is the gate of prohibition (*vāraṇa-mukha*); "practice all that is good" is the gate of exhortation (*anuśāsana-mukha*). The meaning of non-action (*anabhisamskāra*) encompasses both good and evil;

the meaning of the non-action of both good and evil is subsumed within cessation and practice. Now, first we clarify "good": the precept of goodness is simply the non-arising [of evil]; once [evil] has arisen, its eradication is entirely through practice.

The meaning of *śamatha* (cessation) is that which involves stilling, while the meaning of *vipaśyanā* (insight/application) is that which involves progress; thus, the distinction between cessation and application arises from following the strength or weakness [of the mind].

Following the arising of the mind to cease evil and produce non-action is cessation (*śamatha*); following the arising of the mind to cultivate good and produce non-action is application (*vipaśyanā*).
Examples of the non-action of good include constructing wells and bridges, prostrating to the Buddha, and practicing giving; examples of the non-action of evil include constructing fishing nets.

Hunting and the like are non-virtuous non-informative actions (*avijñapti*). Next, regarding the two types of non-informative action—those of the path (*mārga*) and meditative concentration (*samādhi*)—there are both movement and stillness.

The ethical discipline (*śīla*) of the path and meditative concentration is judged as "stillness," while the mental states of the path and meditative concentration are judged as "movement. Regarding the arising of non-informative action from these:

after the cessation of conditions for movement, non-informative action arises from the subsequent cessation of conditions for stillness; this is the goodness of stillness. From the conditions for movement... [non-informative action arises].

The non-manifesting (avijñapti) that arises after the cessation [of manifest action] is called "active goodness" (*kriyā-kuśala*). Furthermore, the gate of prohibition (*pratiṣedha-mukha*) constitutes "stopping goodness" (*saṃvara-kuśala*), while the gate of exhortation (*anuśaṃsana-mukha*) entirely belongs to "active goodness.

Alternatively, it is explained that practice (*caryā*) consists solely of manifestation, whereas stopping (*saṃvara*) consists solely of non-manifestation. It is also said that both the goodness of stopping and the goodness of practice possess non-manifestation.
The seven classes of precepts for śrāvakas are all the essence of the restraint-precept (*saṃvara-śīla*), yet they consist merely of the stopping of body and speech.
The *pāpa-bodhisattva-saṃvara* (evil bodhisattva vow) fully guards the three karmas; furthermore, it extends [the application] up to the Buddha, with differences in length and breadth.
Regarding the meaning of *avijñapti* (non-informative action), it increases following conditions. A superior mind (*adhimātra-citta*) gives rise to it, whereas an inferior mind does not.

An indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) mind, being weak, does not give rise to *avijñapti*. Just as the afflictions (*kleśa*) of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) have nine grades, the first six grades give rise to *avijñapti*.

Because the latter three categories do not arise, it is said that a *sakṛdāgāmin* emerges from the non-manifest (*avijñapti*) of the indeterminate, an *anāgāmin* emerges from the non-manifest of the unwholesome, and an arhat emerges from the non-manifest of the neutral.
This is discussed in relation to the mind of wholesome and unwholesome non-manifest action, each having four permutations.
Regarding the four permutations of the wholesome: first, there is the precept which is not non-manifest; it is so called because the mind that ceases evil is capable of restraint.

First, it is morality (*śīla*) but not non-informative action (*avijñapti*); this refers to the construction of wells, bridges, and so forth, which, according to the specific act and its utility, consist of non-informative action and the like that cannot prevent evil, and thus are not morality.
Second, it is both morality and non-informative action; this refers to the virtuous restraints (*kuśala-saṃvara*) and so forth.

Third, it is neither morality nor non-informative action; this refers to other virtuous mental states. Regarding the four permutations (*catuṣkoṭi*) of immoral conduct (*duḥśīla*), [the same structure applies].

First, there is that which is a precept but not non-manifest action (*avijñapti*), namely the cessation of a virtuous mind. Second, there is that which is non-manifest action but not a precept, namely the non-manifest action arising from acts such as killing or stealing.
Third, there is that which is both a precept and non-manifest action, namely the unwholesome vows (*akuśala-saṃvara*) and so forth.

Fourth, there is that which is neither a precept nor non-manifest action, namely other unwholesome states of mind. There are two types of unwholesome precepts: first, the sixteen unwholesome [courses of action].
Regarding the two types of restraint, the wrong precepts (*mithyā-śīla*) of non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) and the evil restraints (*duḥśīla*) are as described in the *Mahā-sūtra*.

Among the ninety-five kinds of non-Buddhist evil precepts, each has its own system of rules: some take ascetic practices as their precepts, while others maintain the observance of cows, horses, and so forth;

they worship fire, wear [skins], constantly stand on one foot, leap into fire, or throw themselves from cliffs—taking these very acts as their precepts, which constitute wrong precepts. Following [these]...
To direct the mind toward either long or short [lifespans] is entirely a violation of the precepts.
○ Third, the detailed analysis is further divided into three parts: first, one must have faith; second, there must be no three obstructions; third, persons and dharmas serve as conditions.
Regarding "faith," based on the gateway of the Tripiṭaka, three types are briefly enumerated: first, faith in cause and effect—that good and evil necessarily [yield their respective results].
There are three things to be summoned: first, the conviction that by attaining penetration into the Truths, one can contemplate the Truths and will certainly attain the Noble Path;
second, the conviction that there is precept, for this contemplation of the Truths is the initial gateway to entering the Path, and it relies upon the Mahāvaipulya precepts;

therefore, one should be prepared with these three convictions. Furthermore, add another three kinds: first, the conviction that the mind-consciousness of both oneself and others possesses Buddha-nature; second, the conviction that one should diligently practice supreme goodness.

One will certainly be able to attain the fruit; the fruit obtained through the three faiths is characterized by permanence, bliss, self, and purity. Next, regarding those without the three obstructions: sentient beings have three kinds of obstructions.
Because afflictions (*kleśa*) are ever-present, they are not specifically termed "obstructions. As for karmic obstructions (*karma-āvaraṇa*), there are light and heavy varieties.

Heavy karmic obstructions refer to the violation of the precepts (*śīla*), which obstructs the cause [of liberation]. This refers to the seven heinous acts (*ānantarya*) and the ten grave offenses (*daśa-guru-karma*), which exist in one's present life.
This constitutes an obstruction such that the previous life can no longer be known; the events of a separated birth are distant. Regarding the seven heinous offenses (*ānantarya*):

one view holds that they are extinguished through repentance and thus do not constitute an obstruction; another view holds that whether one repents after committing one or more of them, all are obstructions. Regarding the ten heavy precepts:

one view holds that the first four are natural transgressions (*prakṛti-sāvadya*) whose nature is identical to the seven heinous offenses, and thus whether one repents or not, they all constitute obstructions; furthermore, for these six, repentance does not remove the obstruction.

1. Regarding the obstruction of non-regret, it obstructs two [of the ten]. It is said that the first four must involve regret, whereas the characteristics of the latter six do not constitute obstructions even if there is no regret.
2. It is said that non-regret for all ten grave offenses constitutes an obstruction; once regret has been felt, none of them constitute an obstruction. 3.

As for the "obstruction of retribution" (*vipāka-āvaraṇa*), it refers to being naturally separated from the heavy sufferings of the two realms of hell-beings and hungry ghosts. Judging by the majority of precedents, this is not stated to be a cause [for other obstructions].
Humans and animals that are capable of understanding speech are all able to receive the precepts. Non-humans—such as ghosts, spirits, asuras, and nāgas—are considered animals.

Among humans, both men and women, eunuchs, and those with dual sexual organs [may receive them]. As for devas, from the six heavens of the desire realm up to the eighteen Brahma heavens, they are all said to be "causes" [of rebirth].
Since those in the four formless attainments can hear the Dharma, they too should be able to receive my [precepts]; it is merely a matter of karma.

Because its retribution is empty and subtle, the perversion of grasping at the "sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception" (naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana) is not mentioned here in brief. If one turns the mind toward the wholesome, one can also obtain the precepts.
The Sūtra states that the three miserable realms, long-lived heavens, and the borderlands are "difficult places" (durgati), based on the sense that the Path cannot be cultivated there.

The *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-vibhāṣā* records that when dragons and others receive the eightfold fast (aṣṭāṅga-upavāsa), they merely obtain wholesome merit but do not receive the name of "fast" (upavāsa).

Now, reasoning from the text, since the five precepts are the foundation of the bodhisattva precepts and do not manifest the definitive discipline of the Buddha-dharma, it is permitted that they may be attained through all four modes of birth.

From the eight precepts up to the full precepts (*upasampadā*), these manifest the definitive majestic deportment of the renunciant; thus, they can only be induced among humans in the three continents, and not in other realms.

None of these are [the sole] causes. In the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, it is said that the dragon immediately obtained the eight precepts of the upavāsa. Next, regarding the conditions for persons and dharmas:

first, concerning the conditions of persons, there are three ways one obtains the bodhisattva precepts: from the Buddhas, from holy beings, or from ordinary teachers. Regarding the Buddhas, there are two types:
first, the true Buddha, such as when Prince Miaohai received the bodhisattva precepts from Vairocana Buddha; second...

Regarding images of the Buddha made of gold, copper, clay, wood, or other materials, if there is no teacher within a thousand *li* to grant permission, one may seek auspicious signs and undergo self-vow ordination.
Relics such as bone fragments (*śarīra*), hair, nails, alms bowls, staffs, and teeth should all be treated with profound reverence; they can all serve as conditions for practice.
However, as it is difficult to distinguish whether relics are authentic or not, if they are those of a minor saint who is revered as if he were the Buddha, one may rely upon them accordingly.
Regarding the Mahāyāna sūtra scroll, there are three interpretations: first, it states that [receiving precepts] is not permitted;

second, it states that if one lacks a teacher for a distance of a thousand *li*, one may receive them by facing a Buddha image; if one lacks a Buddha image for a distance of a thousand *li*, one may receive them by facing a sūtra scroll;
third, it states that regardless of whether a Buddha exists or not, one may take a Mahāyāna sūtra scroll as the object of focus (*ālambana*) for receiving the Mahāyāna precepts.
Wherever [this scripture] is located, it is no different from a Buddha-stūpa. Furthermore, there are two kinds of "sages": first, the true sage; second, the image sage.

The "true" refers to great beings (mahāsattvas) of the ten stages (*bhūmi*) and above, who serve as the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) for this [practice]; thus, one should generate the precepts in their presence.
The "image" sage refers to images of Bodhisattvas made of gold, copper, and so forth. This sutra also states that one should take the vow before the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.

If one fears that receiving the precepts with only an image of a Bodhisattva would result in a superficial or empty practice—just as when an ordinary person resolves their mind [on enlightenment], they too act as a Bodhisattva—then this person’s image cannot be used for the words of receiving the precepts. This is because "Buddha-Bodhisattvas" refers to Bodhisattvas existing within the presence of a Buddha;

the *Bodhisattvabhūmi* merely speaks of images of Buddhas and does not mention Bodhisattvas. Third, regarding the "ordinary masters," there are those who are ordinary beings within the mundane realm (*pṛthagjana*).
Those outside the ranks of the ordinary practitioners (bāi-fán) all take a True Person (zhēn-rén) as their object of reliance; the use of images is not permitted.

In the sutras, they are called "wise ones" (*jñānin*). Regarding the number of teachers: according to the *Dìchí jīng* (*Bodhisattvabhūmi-sūtra*) and the *Yíngluò jīng*, there is only one teacher; in the *Fǎnwǎng jīng*, the reception of the Dharma likewise involves only one teacher.

Furthermore, because the prohibitions against the seven heinous offenses (*saptānantarya*) within the lower precepts refer to the Upādhyāya and Ācārya, it is evident that there was no practice of formally requesting an Upādhyāya.
Regarding the mention of the *upādhyāya* (preceptor) in the Dharma, this refers to the Buddhas as the preceptors.
Although the text states that the two masters should ask, "Do you have any of the seven obstructing offenses (*saptāvaraṇa*)?", this does not mean they do not refer to the Buddhas.

Even when a wise person is present, one should still perform the rite together before an image of the Buddha or before a scripture to assist in its initiation. At that time, the wise person [stands] before the Buddha image.
If there was previously a wise person who did not possess scriptures or images, they would not have been able to receive the precepts;

for among the eighteen articles required, it is prescribed that images of the Buddha and scriptures must always be kept together. Next, regarding the discussion of virtuous deeds, the *Brahmajāla Sūtra* states that one who acts as a teacher must necessarily be an ordained bodhisattva endowed with five virtues:
first, upholding the precepts; second, having twenty years of seniority (*lǎ*); third, understanding...

The Vinaya-piṭaka exhausts the four [dhyānas] and the contemplation of the five wisdoms; its profound mysteries were transmitted by Master Kumārajīva and transcribed by Master Tanyong, and have been passed down to the present day—this is the orthodox teaching. Next, the *Bhūmivastu* states:

"One must possess precepts and virtue that are strict and luminous, be well-versed in the Tripiṭaka, and be capable of inspiring reverence in others before one may receive [the precepts]; otherwise, one incurs an offense."
