Next, regarding the discussion of the methods for the Dharma-precepts used by both monastics and laypeople, six versions are briefly presented:

first, the Brahmajāla-sūtra version; second, the Yogācārabhūmi version; third, the Gaochang version; fourth, the Avataṃsaka version; fifth, the newly compiled version; and sixth, the Zhiyi (Zizhi) version.
The *Upāsaka-śīla-sūtra* is specifically conferred upon the laity, while the method for receiving the precepts in the *Samantabhadra-bodhisattva-dhyāna-sūtra* largely resembles [the former].
Regarding the method for high-ranking individuals to personally vow to receive the Dharma, it is not listed here in full detail.

This *Brahmajāla Sūtra* method for receiving the precepts was bestowed by Vairocana Buddha upon Prince Miaohai; Śākyamuni received it from Vairocana and subsequently recited it, transmitting it in turn to Bodhisattva Yīduó (Mañjuśrī).
In this manner, it was passed down in succession through more than twenty bodhisattvas until it reached Master Kumārajīva.
To proceed with the extraction from the *Vinaya-piṭaka*: First, receive the Three Refuges, saying:

Next, perform the threefold binding of the precepts (recite three times). Next, repent for the ten unwholesome karmas (rise again to perform three prostrations). Next, praise and accept [the precepts].
Exhort them to listen attentively (recited three times). Directly explain the ten grave precepts and ask whether they can uphold them (responding in order that they "can").
Thereafter, summarize and praise them, and make vows. For anything else not yet understood, they may question the Precept Master (and then the assembly disperses). The subsequent text states:
"Those who wish to receive the precepts should, with incense and lamps, invite one master to come before the Buddha to receive them. The master should ask: 'Can you endure the ten matters?'"

Practices such as cutting one's own flesh to feed a hawk or casting oneself before a starving tiger (it is feared that only those at the stage of the *śuklavidarśana-bhūmi* or above could perform such acts) are also described;

it is said that within a thousand *li*, if no teacher is available, one may take the three refuges by making a self-vow before an image of the Buddha, performing repentance, and reciting the ten grave precepts exactly as previously stated, differing only in being spoken aloud.
It is traditionally held that the *Dìchí jīng* (*Bodhisattvabhūmi-sūtra*) was spoken by Maitreya, and its original source is [the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*].

The Buddha Dīpaṃkara spoke the *Lotus-Treasury Bodhisattva’s Recitation* (*Padmagarbha-bodhisattva-parigraha*). Following this, more than thirty other bodhisattvas successively transmitted and transformed [beings].
Subsequently, the bodhisattva Īśvara manifested his traces and relied upon transformation to transmit [this teaching] to this land.

Xiao Er further redoubled his sincerity in performing rites of repentance for three years from beginning to end. One night, he dreamed that Śākyamuni Buddha conferred the precepts upon him.

"One who receives the Bodhisattva precepts shall transcend the four māras and surmount the suffering of the three realms; in every birth, they shall never lose the constant following of the practitioner."
Upon attaining Buddhahood, if one has not received the precepts, one is not called a sentient being with consciousness;

such a person is no different from those who have permanently departed from the ocean of the Triple Gem—they are non-Bodhisattvas, followers of heterodox paths with false views, and devoid of human sentiment.

To exhort others to receive the precepts brings merit superior to that of constructing eighty-four thousand jeweled stupas. Furthermore, a Bodhisattva who possesses the precepts—even if they commit an offense—is superior to one who lacks the precepts and remains unoffended. If...

Receiving [the precepts] before a true Buddha or Bodhisattva is called the superior grade of precept. If, after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, one receives them from a former teacher within a thousand *li* where no Buddha or Bodhisattva is present, it is called the middle grade of precept.
If, within a thousand *li*, there is no Dharma master, one makes a vow before an image of the Buddha or Bodhisattva to receive them; this is called the inferior grade of precept. (Five New)
The compiler of this text has gathered the practices of various masters of recent times into eighteen sections.

First, the master enters the ritual hall and prostrates to the Buddha, then takes his seat beside the Buddha. Second, the disciple enters the ritual hall, prostrates to the Buddha, and kneels with the right knee on the ground (*huku*).
Third, the master invokes the Triple Gem. Fourth, he instructs [the disciple] to arouse the thought that the Triple Gem is as if present before one's eyes.
Fifth: Confession of the ten unwholesome karmas; Sixth: Requesting the noble ones to act as preceptors;
Seventh: Requesting the present preceptor; Eighth: The preceptor’s praise of the disciple’s ability to generate the supreme mind;
Ninth: Properly begging for these precepts; Tenth: Instruction on generating the bodhicitta; Eleventh: Inquiry regarding obstructive factors (fifteen questions); Twelfth.
13. Contemplating the Attainment of the Precepts; 14. Taking the Vow at the Time of Generating the Precepts; 15.

Receiving the Three Refuges of the Bodhisattva (generating the precepts by means of these three refuges); 16. The Master Rising to Intone the *Karmavācanā* (also generating the precepts by means of the *karmavācanā*);
17. Concluding the Ceremony; 18. The Master Returning to His Seat and Exhorting Study; 19. Explaining the Characteristics of the Ten Grave Offenses, Summarizing, and Praising.
Having sighed and paid obeisance, he departed. The Six Imperial Decrees on the Method for Receiving Precepts fully contain the procedures for both lay and monastic practitioners;
as the text is extensive, it is not listed here.
The Bodhisattva Precept Sūtra.
The title of this sutra is *Brahmajāla* (The Brahma’s Net), the upper fascicle.

The text states that the Buddha, observing how the thousandfold layers of Indra’s net possess variegated colors that do not obstruct one another, taught that the infinite worlds are like the meshes of the net;
each world is distinct from the others, and the various gateways of the Buddhas’ teachings are likewise adorned as a Brahma-net.

The body is without obstruction; its name is established through analogy as a general metaphor for the various and differing meanings expounded throughout this entire treatise, which is like the net of Brahmā.
The title of the chapter, "The Bodhisattva’s Ground of the Mind," is likewise an analogical name. What is elucidated within this chapter constitutes the essential function of the Mahāsattva:
just as the human body possesses a heart that can coordinate all affairs and give rise to superior fruits, so too does this ground serve its purpose.
Regarding the meaning of being the basis for Great Beings (mahāsattva), it is said to be like the earth. *Vairocana* is translated in the *Ratnarāśi Sūtra* as "Pure and Full" (*jingman*):
he is called "Pure" because all afflictions have been completely exhausted, and he is called "Full" because all virtues are perfectly complete.
*Śākyamuni* is translated in the *Śrī-samparigraha Sūtra* as "Capable Sage" (*nengrou*), also called "Capable Benevolence" (*nengren*), and further "Capable of Endurance" (*nengren*).
He is also called the Muni of the Straight Forest, whose body, speech, and mind are perfected; alternatively, he is called the One Who Crosses the Vojā (the Sea of Desolation).
These are different explanations. In the "Chapter on Names" of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, he is named Rocana or Śākyamuni;

here we clarify that they are neither identical nor different, being merely what is appropriate for various capacities and conditions to hear. Śākyamuni preached [this] while residing in the palace of Maheśvara in the fourth dhyāna heaven.

In this "Chapter on the Mind-Ground," examining the text from beginning to end, there are one thousand Śākyamunis and a thousand billion Śākyamunis, each connecting with those with whom they have a karmic affinity, all of whom proceed to the presence of Vairocana to receive the Bodhisattva Precept-piṭaka;

subsequently, each sits at a site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*) to manifest the attainment of perfect awakening and reiterates the preaching of the Dharma across ten locations. The first is at the Hall of Sublime Light, where he preaches the Ten [Great Vows].
1. In the Ocean of Worlds, [the Buddha] spoke the Ten Abodes (daśabhūmi) in the palace of Śakra; 2. In the Yāma heaven, he spoke the Ten Practices (daśacaryā); 3.
In the Tuṣita heaven, he spoke the Ten Dedications (daśapariṇāmanā); 4. In the Nirmāṇarati heaven, he spoke the Ten Meditative Concentrations (daśadhyāna);
5. In the Paranirmita-vaśavartin heaven, he spoke the Ten Grounds (daśabhūmi); 6. In the First Dhyāna, he spoke the Ten Vajras (daśavajra); 7. In the Second [Dhyāna],...

In the *Dhyāna* section, ten kinds of patience (*kṣānti*) are taught, nine of which are situated in the third dhyāna; ten kinds of vows (*praṇidhāna*) are taught, ten of which are situated in the fourth dhyāna.

In the "Chapter on the Mind-Ground" (*Cittabhūmi-paṭala*), the tenth assembly, these three sets of ten minds and ten stages (*bhūmi*) are further explained collectively according to the principle of signlessness (*animitta*).
Furthermore, it is subsequently stated that Śākyamuni entered from the initial Lotus Treasury World (*Padmagarbha-lokadhātu*) into the celestial palaces and descended to Jambudvīpa.
The attainment of the Way and the title Śākyamuni began at the site of enlightenment with the preaching of the Dharma;

this continued through ten locations, and finally, descending from the celestial palace to beneath the Bodhi tree, he preached for the sake of these sentient beings the precepts first recited by Vairocana upon his initial aspiration—namely, the ten grave and forty-eight light precepts. The text as explained in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* has not yet been fully transmitted; it currently exists only in fragments.
In this sutra, there are many accounts of [the Buddha] rising from his seat and proceeding to other locations across seven places and eight assemblies;
yet it is not stated that he remained seated while teaching the Dharma in the Nirmāṇarati Heaven. Furthermore, it describes him teaching the ten dhyāna-concentrations while in the Nirmāṇarati Heaven.

Moreover, the various stages (bhūmis) are largely inconsistent, with the seating arrangements sometimes differing or being identical across preceding and succeeding sections. This is truly because the traces of the Sage are difficult to fathom.
These various explanations are merely given according to the differing capacities of beings; within the Three Teachings, they constitute the Sudden Teaching.

It clarifies that the wondrous principle of the One Vehicle—the eternally abiding Buddha-nature—is intended solely for the Mahāsattvas and not for those of the Two Vehicles. As the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states:

"The followers of the Two Vehicles were in the assembly, yet they neither knew nor perceived [this], because the stages and positions of the Mahāsattvas are not within the sphere of practice of the Two Vehicles. Thus it is restricted.
Regarding the gravity of the precepts, these are not what is studied in the Hīnayāna; the disciplinary regulations for the precepts of the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna differ.

For Bodhisattvas, fifty-eight matters are regulated all at once and simultaneously, whereas for Śrāvakas, they are established according to the commission of an offense. This discussion concerning the principles of the occasion and the suitability of the capacity has three meanings:
first, the Great Being possesses deep faith and does not reject hearing [the teachings] all at once, while the Śrāvaka possesses shallow faith and cannot hear them all at once.

First, regarding the fact that [the precepts] were not received upon hearing them: the Mahāsattvas did not constantly attend [the Buddha] at his side, nor was there a constant reporting of matters as they arose;

therefore, the rules were established all at once. Śrāvakas, however, could always attend him, and since they might have few desires and report matters to the Buddha, the rules were established only after an offense had occurred.
Third, regarding what is prescribed in the *Brahmajāla-sūtra*: it originated when Vairocana, for the sake of Prince Miaohai (Sudhana), bestowed [the precepts].
Regarding the Bodhisattva Precepts: at that time, because it was necessary to explain these fifty-eight types of dharmas for all the Great Beings (Mahāsattvas), they were established all at once.
The *Fanwang* (Brahmajāla) Mahā-sūtra consists of one hundred and twelve fascicles and sixty-one chapters;

only the tenth chapter, the "Bodhisattva Mind-Ground Chapter," was recited and brought forth by Master Kumārajīva in two fascicles (upper and lower). The upper fascicle contains the preface on the stages of the bodhisattva.
This work, belonging to a lower rank, clarifies that the Bodhisattva precepts originate from the Great Root [Sūtra]; both its introduction and its concluding transmission (pariṇāmanā) are missing.
Since it is a separate section yet is titled the *Bodhisattvabhūmi-saṃvara-śīla-sūtra*, it is treated as such.

Regarding the text itself, it is divided into three parts: first, from the initial verse through the prose section ending with "pure," this constitutes the introduction; next, from the ten grave [offenses]... [text ends].
The present Bodhisattva now recites this as the formal exposition (*samyag-deśanā*), while the remainder of the entire fascicle serves as the exhortation for its circulation.
Regarding the introduction, the first verse clarifies the inspiration of Vairocana, while the prose section clarifies the inspiration urged by Śākyamuni.
In the verse, the general meaning consists of four precepts and three exhortations. As for the four precepts: first, the precept of Vairocana; second, the precept of Śākyamuni.
The three types of bodhisattva precepts and the four types of sentient-being precepts take Samantabhadra as their essence; Śākyamuni is the manifestation through whom they are transmitted.
Having attained these, Śākyamuni further bestowed them upon all bodhisattvas; having attained these precepts, the bodhisattvas in turn transmitted them to ordinary sentient beings.
Regarding the three exhortations: first, the exhortation to receive; second, the exhortation to uphold; and third, the exhortation to recite these four categories of precepts.
There is a specific reason for obtaining this: it was transmitted from the fundamental source through a profound lineage, bestowed from below as a prediction of Buddhahood (*buddha-vyākaraṇa*).

Thus, it encourages ordinary beings to receive it; once received, it must be maintained; once maintained, it must be recited. This is intended so that its transmission may continue without interruption.
The eleven and a half lines of verse are divided into three sections. The first three lines and phrases clarify Śākyamuni’s preaching of the precepts and their transmission.

Regarding Śākyamuni: from "At this time, [there were] hundreds of thousands of koṭis" down to the third line and third phrase, it clarifies how the trace-Buddha Śākyamuni transmitted [the teaching] to the various bodhisattvas, and how those bodhisattvas transmitted it to sentient beings.

From "Listen attentively as I correctly recite" down to the end of the verse, it clarifies the exhortation to believe, accept, and uphold [the teaching]. As for the three sequences: these three Buddhas each spoke two [parts].
It is said that the first introduction was spoken by Vairocana himself, while the other two were spoken here in this land by Śākyamuni;
however, it is now stated that all three introductions were spoken here in this land by Śākyamuni, interspersed with the words of the sūtra compiler.

The first section is further divided into two parts: the first two lines and a half clarify the fundamental and the manifested (honji-suijaku), while the subsequent one line and a phrase clarify the person and the Dharma.
Regarding the first part, there are again three sections: the first half-line clarifies the essential body of Vairocana;
the next one line and a half clarify the manifested Buddha Śākyamuni; and the final half-line summarizes the fundamental and the manifested.
"I, now as Vairocana, sit upon the lotus pedestal.
The first phrase clarifies the original body of Śākyamuni (Śākyamuni’s *svabhāva-kāya*), while the second phrase clarifies the original land of Śākyamuni.

This refers to the fourfold aspects of the Buddha-body, comprising both the primary and secondary retributions (*dharmakāya*, *sambhogakāya*, *nirmāṇakāya*, and *samyaksambuddha*). Specifically: first, the *dharmakāya*; second, the true and the responsive; third, the *dharmakāya*, *sambhogakāya*, and *nirmāṇakāya*.
The Dharmakāya is the body of the pervasive radiance of the True Dharma; the Sambhogakāya is the body of the fruition resulting from the fulfillment of practices;

and the Nirmāṇakāya is the body that manifests traces in response to the needs of beings. The *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-śāstra* names these the Dharma-body and the Response-body (Nirmāṇakāya). Furthermore, regarding the four bodies:
the Response-body receives the offering of Cunda, while the Transformation-body receives the offerings of the great assembly. As for me now, I am the eightfold self-mastering one.
"Amitābha" (also known as *Amitāyus*) signifies that his ignorance and defilements have been forever exhausted, and his wisdom and merit are perfectly complete, like the pure full moon;
thus, the name expresses his virtue. The phrase "sitting upon a lotus flower" below clarifies his *pariṇāmanā-vipāka* (recompensed environment). "Square" (*fang*) means "correct" (*zheng*);
because he dwells securely in the True Dharma, it is called "sitting. Why does he sit upon a lotus pedestal? It is because the shape of the world resembles it.
Because it is a lotus, it is called the "Lotus Treasury. The *Avataṃsaka* states that "the flower is below, supporting the lotus," which carries two meanings:

first, being situated in filth without being defiled, which is an analogy for Vairocana dwelling in impurity without being stained; second, "treasury" (*garbha*) signifies that the ten directions and the entire dharma-realm are all contained within it;
and "pedestal" (*maṇḍala*) signifies the center, representing that the cause is able to give rise to the fruit, thus serving as an analogy for the pedestal. Furthermore, by means of...
The original Buddha seated upon the lotus pedestal further symbolizes that the precepts are the foundation of all virtues.
Upon the thousand petals surrounding [the central one], there again appear a thousand Śākyamunis;
on each of the ten billion lands within a single petal, there is a Śākyamuni, each sitting beneath a Bodhi tree, simultaneously attaining the Way of Buddhahood.

Surrounding these are one thousand Śākyamunis, who look toward ten billion lands. Of these, the one thousand Śākyamunis constitute the "essence" (hon), while the ten billion constitute the "manifestation" (shaku).

Thus, there are two layers of essence and manifestation. This, in turn, comprises three parts: first, clarifying the essence within the manifestation; second, clarifying the manifestation within the manifestation;
and third, clarifying that both the essence and the manifestation all achieve the Buddha-way. Now, for the first part, clarifying the essence within the manifestation, there are one thousand...
The flower is the flower among humans, possessing more than ten petals; the flower among devas has a hundred petals;
and the flower of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas has a thousand petals. Because each petal represents one Buddha-world, there are thus a thousand Buddha-pure lands.

This signifies the fundamental ground where the causes of the ten stages and ten pāramitās are perfected, giving rise to the fruit of responsive manifestation. It manifests the one thousand Śākyamunis, with each petal representing one pure land.
This is precisely one Buddha-world manifesting the perfect response-body (*nirmāṇakāya*). Furthermore, within another world, there is one Buddha-land;
this is a brief description of the *Avataṃsaka*’s worlds as numerous as motes of dust, with one hundred such worlds in each of the ten directions.
Regarding "one flower contains ten billion lands": the following two points clarify the traces-within-traces. On a single petal is one world, and within it are ten billion [lands].
The Sahā world-system consists of ten billion lands, which are but a single leaf; each sits beneath it, having attained the Buddha-way through both their original and manifested forms.
This clarifies that within the manifested realm, both the original and the manifested have all attained the Buddha-way.
"Thus, the thousands, hundreds, and ten-thousands of millions [of manifestations]...
This third summary of the primary and secondary aspects of Vairocana’s own body concludes the initial phrase regarding the secondary body and the subsequent phrase regarding the primary body,
clarifying that all thousands, hundreds, and ten-thousands of millions take Vairocana as their source.
II. Second, the clarification of persons and dharmas is divided into two sections according to the text: first, the clarification of persons; second, the clarification of dharmas.
"The thousands of billions of Śākyamunis, Each receiving as many beings as atoms of dust, All come together to my abode.
Regarding persons, there are three phrases: first, clarifying the person who receives; second, clarifying the persons who are received; third, [the capacity].
The one who receives and those who are received together arrive at the Buddha’s dwelling; the person who is received is the thousand-billion Śākyamunis.

Each "receives" according to their capacity; "receiving" (jie) signifies the meaning of taking hold of those with whom there is a karmic affinity. "Dust-like" (weichen) refers to the great number of listeners.
They all come together, as described below in the third section, which concludes that both the receiver and the received have arrived together.
At the abode of Śākyamuni Buddha, listen as I recite the Buddha’s precepts. The gate of ambrosia is now opened.

[Verse 2] Regarding the two lines on the Dharma of Illumination: first, the illumination of the recitation of the precepts; next, the formal praise of the precepts. First, the admonition for Bodhisattvas.
Question: Regarding those who listen and recite the Buddha’s precepts, why do they only recite them and not explain their meaning?

Answer: These are the dharmas of the Buddhas of the three periods and ten directions; they were not created by oneself for the first time. Therefore, one may only "recite" them, but cannot "explain" them.
As for the "Gate of Ambrosia," this praises the precepts as being like ambrosia, which enables people to attain longevity and immortality; it is essential to rely upon this.
The precepts lead to Nirvana—eternal, blissful, self, and pure; the teaching can penetrate the principle, being like a gate.
Furthermore, the precepts can rescue and deliver one from birth and death, like the nectar of immortality (amṛta) which, when consumed, grants long life. A great sūtra says:
"If mountains were to come from the four directions, one should only maintain the precepts and practice giving."

○ At this time, the "thousand times ten million" [Buddhas] below [the first section] constitutes the second part: the transmission from Śākyamuni, the Buddha of Traces, to the Bodhisattvas, and the transmission from the Bodhisattvas to sentient beings.
This further consists of three parts: first, clarifying the causes and conditions for Śākyamuni Buddha’s transmission as narrated by the scriptural masters;
second, clarifying how Śākyamuni preached the precepts and transmitted them to the various Bodhisattvas; third, exhorting the Bodhisattvas to transmit and transform others.
At that time, the thousands of myriads of koṭis of sentient beings returned to their original places of enlightenment and each sat beneath a bodhi tree.
Now, first, the sūtra author describes the origins of Śākyamuni’s transmission; these three lines clarify that each of the thousands of myriads of koṭis of Buddhas [performed this].
Return to your original place and recite the precepts of our Original Teacher: The ten grave and forty-eight minor precepts Are like the sun and moon, and also like a jeweled necklace.
By means of these, the multitude of bodhisattvas as numerous as motes of dust Attain perfect enlightenment.
This is what Vairocana recites; I likewise recite it in this way. You, newly initiated Bodhisattvas, should receive and uphold these precepts upon the crown of your heads.

Since the Dharma-body does not exist [in form], we now clarify the traces: the transmission of the original precepts takes the original as the teacher of the traces, and the traces as the teacher of the original.
This is because it is based on the recitation of the original text. The transmission to the various bodhisattvas consists of three parts:
first, clarifying the essence of the precepts; second, clarifying the function of the precepts; and third, exhorting bodhisattvas to receive and uphold the ten major and forty-eight minor precepts.

Regarding the first, clarifying the essence of the precepts: the ten major precepts and so forth constitute the essence of the precepts. "The precepts are like the bright moon" [is the beginning of the second part], praising the function of upholding the precepts.
This precept can dispel the mist of transgressions like the sun; it brings about refreshing coolness like the moon.
It possesses wholesome dharmas like a jeweled necklace; furthermore, just as the sun can cause all things to grow, so too can this precept cause all manner of goodness to flourish.
Moreover, just as a jeweled necklace can alleviate poverty, so too can this precept relieve the suffering of sentient beings.
The poor lack the wealth of the sublime Dharma; yet [the precepts] are like the sun and moon adorning the sky, such that all gaze up in reverence.
When the precepts are embodied, all revere them; when the jeweled necklace is worn upon the body, it is the foremost adornment. To be free from ugliness through the precepts is like being handsome.
Below this, in the third section, there is an exhortation for Bodhisattvas to accept and uphold [the precepts]: just as a person crossing the sea must rely on...

A vessel for crossing over birth and death must depend upon the observance of the precepts. As the Great Sūtra says, it is like relying on a boat or raft, and is further likened to a life-preserving float.

The text is divided into three parts: first, a general statement of its efficacy; second, the clarification of the person who bestows [the precepts]; and third, the clarification of the person who receives them.
"Vairocana" and those following refer to the person who bestows them; "newly initiated students" and those following refer to the person who receives them.
Having received and upheld these precepts, one transmits them to all sentient beings.

This third section, "Receiving and Upholding," encourages the transmission to sentient beings; it concerns the thirty minds of a Bodhisattva who has transmitted [the teachings] to those outside the stages of the ordinary person (*bāhyapṛthagjana*) and has resolved upon the Mahāyāna mind.
The third section, the exhortation to believe and uphold, consists of three parts: first, the presentation of the Dharma to be recited; second, the exhortation for others to believe and accept it;
and third, the concluding exhortation.
Listen attentively as I correctly recite: Within the Buddha-dharma, the treasury of precepts, The Prātimokṣa.
The great assembly believes with a sincere heart: "You shall become a Buddha; I am one who has already become a Buddha.
Always maintaining such faith, the precepts are already fully perfected. All those who possess a mind should receive the Buddha-precepts;
when sentient beings receive the Buddha-precepts, they immediately enter the rank of all Buddhas.
Having attained a station equal to Great Enlightenment, you are truly the children of all Buddhas. The great assembly should all pay respect and listen with a sincere heart as I recite;
listen attentively to the Dharma being recited below. This precept distinguishes [the Buddha's] pure precepts from the precepts of outsiders, such as those of the "chicken" and "dog" sects.
Taking the *vinaya* as the cause and the Great Assembly as the fruit; this is the second section, which encourages others to believe and accept [the teaching], and it is divided into two parts:
first, encouraging belief, and second, encouraging acceptance. Now, for the first part, encouraging belief: the reason it is so is that faith is the initial gateway for entering the Path.
As the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "Faith is that by which one enters; I have upheld these precepts and attained perfect enlightenment, and you should do likewise. (1)
"First, 'All who possess a mind' is the second exhortation to receive [the precepts]. This clarifies that all sentient beings with a mind possess Buddha-nature;
they must certainly become Buddhas and must therefore receive the three precepts of the Bodhisattva Mahāyāna, which are eternal, blissful, and so forth.
Third, 'The great assembly' is the conclusion of the exhortation. The preceding phrase concludes [the section], while the subsequent phrase enjoins them to listen; this explains it in general terms."
The introductory section on the transmission of the precepts by the Buddhas is concluded.

Regarding the prose section below, this introduction concerning Śākyamuni in this land is divided into two parts: first, the words of the sūtra compiler; second, the self-exposition by Śākyamuni himself.
At that time, after Śākyamuni Buddha had first sat beneath the Bodhi tree and attained unexcelled perfect enlightenment, he first formulated the Bodhisattva Prātimokṣa:
the dharma of filial piety toward parents, teachers, and the Triple Gem, and of filial piety toward the Way of Ultimate Truth;
for "filiality" is called precept (*śīla*), and it is also called restraint. Then, the Buddha immediately emitted immeasurable light from his mouth. At that time—
A great assembly of hundreds of billions of bodhisattvas, the eighteen Brahmā heavens, the sons of the gods of the six desire realms,
and sixteen great kings joined their palms and listened with a sincere mind as the Buddha recited the Mahayana precepts of all Buddhas.
The first of the three stages consists of: (1) a general account of the Buddha’s formulation of the precepts; (2) the manifestation of auspicious signs through the emission of light;
and (3) the aspiration of the great assembly to hear [the teaching]. Within the first stage, there are four distinct sections: (1) identifying the Master of Transformation, the Great Sage Śākyamuni;

(2) identifying the location, namely sitting beneath the Bodhi tree—so named because he attained the Way there, thus it is called the "Tree of the Way," and also known as the Pippala tree in the Brahma-language; and (3) [the third section].

The attainment of clear realization refers to the achievement of perfect enlightenment, which is designated as "Right Universal Knowledge" (*samyak-saṃbuddha*). Regarding the dharmas established by the fourfold emergence, these refer to the Bodhisattva Prātimokṣa.
Within the fourth [section], there are four further points: first, the designation of the name of what is established, which is the *mokṣa* (liberation);
second, the superior causes capable of accomplishing it, namely filial service and so forth. As the *Ratnakoṭi Sūtra* states: "Filial service toward one's father..."
The Mother, Lord Śakra, dwells within your home and yet you can practice filial piety;
the Great Brahmā, Honored Deva, dwells within your home and yet you can fulfill filial duty; Śākyamuni Buddha dwells within your home;

and the Bodhisattva Kṣema—the affliction of his own eyes was healed, and the wheel of fire of the Compassionate Child was swiftly extinguished—these are precisely such spiritual responses. The *Erya* says: "Good."
Serving one's parents is filial piety (*xiao*); filial piety is obedience (*shun*). Taishi Shuming used "obedience" to explain "filial piety.

The *Xiaojing Gouming jue* states that the character for "filial piety" (*xiao*) is glossed as "thorough investigation" (*jiu*); "thorough investigation" means to fully understand the beginning and the end, which refers to providing physical care and nourishment. It may also be glossed as "comprehension" (*du*);

"comprehension" refers to ritual propriety, meaning that the practices of warmth and coldness accord with ritual requirements. The Three Illuminations (*sanming*) are able to attain superior fruits, which is called "the ultimate."
The Dharma of the Path consists of four categories; the names of these four are the formulation of the precepts. The Buddha then emitted light from his mouth in successive stages.

This emission of light was a manifestation of an auspicious omen; "omen" (śakuna) signifies faith. Before preaching the Great Matter, it is necessary to emit light, and for this reason it is called an auspicious omen.
Light is the most excellent of all forms and images; by emitting this supreme radiance, he summoned those with karmic affinity to come together and hear the precepts.

Precepts are the most supreme among all virtues, capable of extinguishing evil and giving rise to goodness. The emission of light from the mouth symbolizes that today the World-Honored One Śākyamuni proclaims the Mahāyāna Bodhisattva Precepts.
At that time, ten billion [beings] descended to the lower tier to take their places, wishing to hear the teaching.

The text is divided into three parts: first, a general description of the great assembly; second, a detailed enumeration of the four types of assemblies; and third, [the actual discourse]. The Bodhisattva’s twenty-eight [vows], the three of the Brahma heavens, the six of the desire heavens (kāmadhātu), the forty-six kings, and the three concluding vows—listen now to these.

This section below is the second part, the main exposition. The text is divided into two sections: first, the clarification of the ten major precepts;
second, the forty-eight minor precepts. Regarding the first [section], there are three chapters: first, a general heading; second, a detailed explanation; third, a summary conclusion.
The Buddha addressed the sons of the Buddhas, saying: "There are ten grave *pratimokṣa* precepts.
If one has received the Bodhisattva precepts but does not recite these precepts, they are not a Bodhisattva, nor are they a seed of Buddhahood. I, too, have likewise recited them;

all Bodhisattvas of the past have studied them, all Bodhisattvas of the future shall study them, and all Bodhisattvas of the present are now studying them. Having thus briefly explained the Bodhisattva *prātimokṣa*..."
One should study the characteristics of the Prātimokṣa and uphold it with a reverent mind.
In the general heading, "If one receives the Bodhisattva precepts," the subsequent section excludes what is not [the true path]; "I also recite thus" below clarifies what is indeed [the path].
This is also called "exhorting by citing the fruit. The passage beginning "All Bodhisattvas" clarifies the intent of the three periods of time, encouraging one to reflect upon and emulate them.
To encourage those who receive it, the *Prātimokṣa* is briefly explained as the manifestation of the sudden precepts; how could a verse praising the essence of the precepts exceed this?
It exhorts one to train accordingly and to uphold them with a reverent mind. II. The detailed explanation is divided into ten parts.
○ First, regarding the precept against killing, which is the beginning of the ten grave prohibitions:

if the precept against unchaste conduct were placed first, many people would give rise to transgressions, and because the afflictions bound to the [lower] realms are heavy, it was established [as second].

Although killing is a natural offense (*prakṛti-sāvadya*), it is rare for renunciants to commit this sin and it is easy to prevent; whereas sexual misconduct arises easily, it was therefore established [as first]. As the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: [text follows].

The precepts of the Śrāvakas adjust to human conditions and provide many defenses against the arising of extremes; thus, those [offenses] that arise frequently are treated lightly, while those that arise rarely are subject to heavy regulations.
Regarding sexual misconduct, it is not an intrinsic offense (*prakṛti-sāvadya*) according to their system, whereas killing is an intrinsic offense.
In the Mahāyāna, both are regulated from the outset. As for killing now, because it severs the life of another, the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) continue in succession.
There are sentient beings who, by severing this continuity in the present, are said to be "killed. The *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra* states that obstructing future continuity is termed "killing";
both monastics and laypeople are equally prohibited from it, as in the case of the five precepts and the eight precepts.
Because the Bodhisattva takes compassion as his foundation, he must sever [this continuity]. The seven classes of Bodhisattvas commit the same offense as the Śrāvaka [precepts].

The various schools are largely the same with minor differences. The similarities lie in their common prohibition against killing; the differences concern three matters: first, the difference between what is permitted and what is prohibited;
second, the difference between form and mind; and third, the difference between light and heavy offenses. Regarding the difference between what is permitted and what is prohibited:

a Mahāsattva may kill when he perceives the appropriate opportunity, whereas a Śrāvaka is not permitted to kill even if he perceives such an opportunity. Regarding the difference between form and mind: a Mahāsattva disciplines the mind, while a Śrāvaka disciplines the body.

Third, regarding the difference in gravity: if a Bodhisattva harms his teacher, it constitutes a *ānantarya* (immediate) offense, whereas for a Śrāvaka it does not. Furthermore, the offenses of a Bodhisattva are more grave than those of a Śrāvaka; that is, they are doubly grave.
If a disciple of the Buddha kills on his own, teaches others to kill, employs means to kill, praises killing, or rejoices upon seeing it being committed—then...

From incantations for killing, the causes of killing, the conditions for killing, the methods of killing, and the karmic actions of killing— down to not intentionally killing any living being whatsoever—
this Bodhisattva ought to give rise to a mind of constant compassion, a mind of filial obedience, and employ skillful means to rescue and protect all sentient beings; yet,
if instead he gives rein to his own self-indulgent heart and takes pleasure in killing, this constitutes a *pārājika* offense for that Bodhisattva.

Regarding the offenses, the text is divided into three distinct sections: first, the designation of the person, which states, "If a Buddha’s disciple"; second, the sequential account of the events, which refers to the three enumerated offenses of defeat (*pārājika*) listed in the middle;

and third, the actual offenses themselves. Within the sequential account of the events, there are three parts: first, that which is improper; second, that which is proper; and third, [the conclusion].
Regarding the formulation of the precepts, within the section on the three distinct offenses that should not be committed, the first six lines clarify the matter of killing.

Among these, there are four lines that establish the formation of the karmic act, and the final line uses a light case to illustrate a heavy one. As for the first six: 1. Killing by oneself, meaning taking the life of another through one's own action.

Within the three types of objects—internal form, external form, and both internal and external form—one commits an offense in all cases. 2. Instructing another to kill; the other person likewise... [text continues].

The *Śīlaparivarta* (Discourse on the Precepts) states that verbal instruction constitutes the sin of killing, whereas the actual infliction of a wound does not. The Vinaya sections distinguish many such categories and threads of analysis.
Third, one who kills by instructing another or dispatching a messenger commits the preparatory act (*prayoga*) of killing, namely the four methods such as binding and tethering.
Fourth, one also incurs the offense of killing by praising it. Fifth, "rejoicing" (*anumodana*) refers to encouraging and exhorting [another to kill].
The severance of life is also an offense. Regarding the six types of incantation-killing, this refers to *vīdara* and so forth;
even if other conditions are employed, they all constitute the same offense. Within the Vinaya, fifteen types of killing are clarified, namely:

*utthātā*, *pratyutthātā*, snares, strings, *vidhura*, and so forth, as explained at length in the Vinaya section, and so on. This concludes the second of the three layers concerning the karma of killing.
The characteristics of karma are as follows: the three types of karma that constitute killing are: first, the bodily karma of performing the act oneself;

second, the vocal karma of instructing others or using incantations to create bodily karma; and third, the mental karma of intending to kill spirits or deities and then carrying it out through one's own declaration, thereby creating bodily karma.
These three stages of formation within the conditions are all the meaning of karma. The method of killing refers to the sword.
Since the sword-pit, the snare, and so forth all possess a substantial nature (*dharmatā*), they are termed the "causes" (*hetu*) of killing by way of phenomena.

Regarding the conditions (*pratyaya*) for killing, there are two paths: the direct and the indirect. The primary cause is the murderous intent; the others are conditions because they assist in its accomplishment.
As for the direct [path], the karma consists of four factors: first, a sentient being; second, the perception of a sentient being; third, the act of killing; and fourth, the taking of life.
Regarding the severance of one [root of goodness], there are sentient beings; although they are numerous, they are broadly categorized into three grades.

The first is the superior grade, referring to the Buddhas, noble ones (āryas), parents, and teachers and monks; to harm these constitutes a transgression of immediate retribution (*ānantarya*). Regarding persons who have attained the three fruits, there are two interpretations:
first, some say it is equivalent to immediate retribution because harming a Śrāvaka is already a matter of the utmost gravity; second, others say it constitutes a grave offense.

The Sūtra clarifies that there are three types of killing that result in the killing of those who have attained the three fruits; these cases involve killing while one is still within the intermediate stage and do not constitute killing from a higher stage.

Thus, we know these are not *ānantarya* (immediate) offenses against a Bodhisattva. Regarding the Bodhisattva who has attained the stage of "Understanding Practice" (*adhimukti-caryā*) and above, the aforementioned section of the Great Sūtra refers to them as "Bodhisattvas of fixed destiny" (*niyata-bhūmi*).

Alternatively, "fixed destiny" may be taken to mean those who will no longer produce the mind of the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*), or it may refer to those from the seventh thought-moment (*citta-kṣaṇa*) upward.

It may be considered a transgression. Regarding the mother carrying a fetus: one interpretation says there is no *ānantarya* (immediate) offense; another says it constitutes an *ānantarya*. For a Mahāsattva, this is more serious than for a Śrāvaka.
The middle grade refers to humans and devas who commit the offense with a harmful intent; the lower grade refers to those in the four realms of existence (*catur-gati*). There are two explanations:
first, that it is equal to the grave offenses of a Mahāsattva because their prevention of killing is so severe; as the text says, "all beings... [are protected].

The fact that one who possesses life must not intentionally kill is the proof [of this]. Second, it is said that although one merely commits a minor offense (*āpatti*) within the context of a grave precept, it is simultaneously regulated because [the victim] is not a fit vessel for the Path;
as the text says, "one who possesses life" uses the light case to illustrate the heavy.
Third, there are two types of intent to kill: first, the intent to kill by oneself; second, the intent to kill by commanding another. Regarding the intent to kill by oneself, there are...

There are two types: those involving direct mental engagement (*sākṣāt-citta*) and those involving indirect mental engagement (*parokṣa-citta*). Regarding direct mental engagement, this refers to cases such as indiscriminately setting traps or snares, or indiscriminately burning or boiling [living beings];

these constitute an offense regardless of the three moral natures (*tri-śīla*). If one intends this for that purpose and gives rise to a harmful mind toward that object, it all belongs to direct mental engagement.
Since one has personally confronted the object and the life can no longer continue, even if the intended result was not achieved, it is entirely a formal offense (*maulāpatti*).
If one digs a pit with the intent to stop someone, but that person dies because they were not where they intended to be, it is an offense of the border;

if the purpose was not achieved, it is a minor defilement. If this path was originally a thoroughfare used by many people, and one digs a pit there with the intent to stop them, and someone dies as a result, it is a grave offense.
Because the act of killing is complete and the conditions for harm are fulfilled, the mind returns to its full causal state.

This pertains to the "intermediate" mind (*vyavahita-citta*). For example, if one intends to strike an Easterner but mistakenly strikes a Westerner, and the Westerner had no intention of killing at all, this belongs to the category of the "separated" mind.
There are two moments when the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) is severed: first, in this life; second, in a future life. Regarding this life, there are two cases:
first, committing a grave offense while possessing the precepts; second, severing the life-faculty at the moment the current precepts are relinquished.
If one fails to complete the formal act of ordination (*karmavācanā*), it is a light defilement; at the time of death, the offense is established as previously described.

For a *śrāvaka* who has not yet completed the act at the time of death, the establishment of the offense occurs when they relinquish the full precepts (*upasaṃpadā*) and take the five precepts (*pañca-śīla*), and so forth. Regarding the restoration of the precepts in a future life, there are two types:

first, restoring them through one's own recollection; second, restoring them without one's own recollection. As for those who restore them through their own recollection, this occurs either by relying on the previous momentum or by employing further expedient means.

Regarding the offense of a grave transgression (pārājika) committed before the end of life: because one remembers both the preceding and succeeding moments, it constitutes a grave offense. If one does not remember [the act], yet dies by the force of circumstances, there is still the precept at the time of death;

thus, it is a grave offense. If one employs a deliberate means (upāya), it should be understood that if the previous wound does not result in death, and one does not remember [the act] at the time of the subsequent application of the means, one incurs only a minor defilement (duṣkṛta).
As for the term "life-faculty" (jīvitendriya), according to the Sāṃkhya school, it is distinct [from the physical body].
Neither matter nor mind constitutes the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*); there is no distinction between the *Abhidharmasamaya-prakaraṇa-śāstra* and the Mahāyāna regarding this point.
It is simply the continuous succession and uninterrupted connection of matter and mind that is taken as "life. The *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* is likewise:
the continuous arising of the six bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*) and the six consciousnesses is conventionally designated as "life," extending even to all that exists.
The third point, "Applying the Light to Illustrate the Heavy," constitutes the second stage of this Bodhisattva path and should consist of three phrases:

first, one should constantly abide in a mind of compassion; regarding this, there are two interpretations: the first is that one should study to constantly abide in the Buddha’s arising of compassion;
the second is that the mind should always abide in the ground of compassion. Second, one should possess a mind of filial obedience, upholding the precepts and not causing affliction to others.
Regarding the three modes of protection through skillful means, it is not merely a matter of not causing harm; rather, one must engage with the situation to provide rescue and liberation.

To act otherwise is improper, and thus constitutes an offense. This is also explained in three phrases: first, acting with a licentious mind, which refers to killing out of greed; second, acting with a sense of gratification, which refers to killing out of anger;
and third, the act of killing itself, which refers to the actual execution of the act of taking life. Because these three factors are present, one falls into [an offense].

As with the precept against killing. ○ Second, the precept against stealing (*adattādāna*): taking what is not given. Taking openly what is not given is called "robbery" (*haraṇa*); taking it secretly and in concealment is called "stealing" (*steya*).

By stealing another's *upabhoga-pariṣkāra* (possessions and requisites), one incurs an offense. This precept is violated by all seven classes of practitioners; for the *śrāvaka*, there are five [degrees of gravity].
Among the various [categories], there are similarities and differences. As for the similarities, none of them should involve stealing. As for the differences, there are three:

first, the difference between what is permitted and what is prohibited, such as whether one may or may not take [an object] upon seeing an opportunity; or again, it is said that stealing upon seeing an opportunity is permissible for a Bodhisattva because he lacks a mind of theft, whereas for a Śrāvaka who acts solely for his own salvation, he must necessarily rely on formal rules. For a Bodhisattva, this is not so.
Fearing the retribution of sin, one should simply act if it brings benefit to others;

yet, for a Śrāvaka, stealing the property of the Buddha after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa is considered light, whereas for a Bodhisattva it is always grave. Furthermore, since one ought to provide for the external life of others, how could taking it instead be the mind of a Great Being?
If a Buddha’s disciple steals, teaches others to steal, uses expedient means to steal, praises stealing, or rejoices upon seeing it done—

even including stealing by incantation, through the causes of stealing, the conditions of stealing, the methods of stealing, or the karmic actions of stealing— and even objects belonging to spirits or deities,
or property belonging to bandits, down to a single needle or a blade of grass— one must not intentionally steal. Rather, a Bodhisattva should give rise to filiality toward the Buddha-nature.

If one who possesses a mind of loving-kindness and compassion, constantly aiding all beings to produce merit and happiness, instead steals another's wealth and property, this constitutes a *pārājika* offense for a Bodhisattva.
Within the introductory section of the matter, there are three sets of three; each of these contains three points that should not exist. This is judged according to eleven phrases.

Third: the first [stage] is the sixth, the second is the fourth, and the last is the first; these correspond to the middle [stage], which likewise has three parts as in the text. The *Wenju* (Explanatory Text) is the same as before.

In the case of the precept against killing, the three stages of the middle [path of action] do not apply as they did for theft. Regarding the karma of theft, the second section below specifically clarifies the characteristics of the completion of the karma, which consists of four phrases identical to those before:

the movement of the hand, taking another's object, moving it from its original location, and the completion of the karma of theft. "Karma" (*karma*) refers to volitional construction (*abhisamskāra*).
Regarding "heavy value for the sake of the Dharma," this refers to five *kārsāpaṇa* coins. The Vinaya states that one large copper coin is equivalent to sixteen small coins;

as for the varying values among these coins, the determination is made based on the location where the theft occurred. Some claim that for a Bodhisattva, the offense is grave even for two *māṣaka* coins or more, whereas for a Śrāvaka, it becomes grave only above two coins.
However, such views are not universally accepted today; rather, five coins are taken as the standard.
This severance is grave; the act of stealing from one’s place of residence is certain to occur at this time. Yet, for the Bodhisattva on the second stage, it is clear that he should respond.

This is largely the same as what was stated previously, with only slight differences: whereas previously it was stated that one should respond by learning to abide in the Buddha’s conduct and practice compassion, here it is said that one should practice filial piety and compassion. Because a Bodhisattva should learn these matters, it is called "should" (應).
That which is improper refers to acts such as stealing and killing; this constitutes both the prohibitory and the exhortatory gates.

The prohibition is to refrain from killing and stealing, while the exhortation is to practice goodness, compassion, kindness, filial piety, and the study of the constant practices of the Buddha’s conduct—all of which are wholesome dharmas that constitute filial piety. As for the Buddha-nature, all sentient beings possess it.
The nature of that which is destined to bear fruit is simply defined as being unchanging; however, this contradicts the third fetter, which would otherwise be untenable.
Regarding the handling of the property of the Triple Gem, it is as explained in the Vinaya.
○ The third precept, the prohibition against sexual misconduct, is called "non-Brahmacarya" because it is a base and vulgar matter; thus, it is termed "impure conduct."

Regarding the seven classes of followers, both Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna prohibit the same transgressions, yet there are differences in the extent of these prohibitions: for the five classes of monastics, both the heterodox and the orthodox are prohibited;
for the two classes [of laypeople], only heterodox sexual misconduct is prohibited. The general similarities and differences with those of the Śrāvakas are largely as described previously.

If a Buddha’s disciple engages in sexual misconduct themselves, or teaches others to engage in sexual misconduct— even with any woman— they must not intentionally commit such acts. Whether through the cause of lust, the condition of lust,
the method of lust, or the karma of lust— even with female animals, goddesses, ghosts, spirits, or by engaging in sexual intercourse through improper orifices—
the Bodhisattva should instead give rise to a heart of filial obedience, seeking to save and deliver all sentient beings and bestowing the pure Dharma upon them.
If, on the contrary, one gives rise to sexual desire toward all people without distinction— even with animals, or even with one’s mother,
daughter, sister, or other close relatives— and acts with a heart devoid of compassion, this constitutes a *pārājika* offense for a bodhisattva.
The introductory section on the three stages: first, that which is improper; second, that which is proper; third, the conclusion regarding sexual misconduct.

Those who have left the household life should not engage in it, but should instead train in the pure conduct of Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, no different from what was previously explained in the section on killing. First, "improper" has three distinct points;
within the section on sexual misconduct, there are four phrases clarifying the completion of the karmic act, followed by three phrases illustrating minor offenses.
Moreover, the repetition of the text contains minor discrepancies and lacks proper sequence; this precept is established as a grave offense (*sthūlātyaya*) when three conditions are met:

first, the path (the anus); second, a lustful mind; and third, the completion of the act. Alternatively, it is established as grave when five conditions are met: first, a sentient being; second, the perception of that being as such;

and so forth, with the final three phrases citing inferior cases to conclude the transgression—namely, intercourse with one's own wife via an improper path, in an improper place, after childbirth, while nursing an infant, or during pregnancy.

In the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* and other such treatises, these are all termed "sexual misconduct. The *Upāsaka-śīla-sūtra* states that among the six grave precepts, sexual misconduct is regulated;

furthermore, within the precept against sexual misconduct, it prohibits improper times and places. This seems to imply that even with one's own wife, engaging in intercourse at an improper time constitutes a grave offense.

If one incites another to commit adultery, while one remains personally free from delusion or defilement, one merely commits a minor stain (*mṛdula-kṣudra-āpatti*). Some say that for a Bodhisattva, this is grave; here, I shall explain the meaning of the sound [of the term].
I have heard that for Bodhisattvas, these cases are not treated in the same manner as killing or stealing.

Whether it be humans, animals, ghosts, spirits, men, women, eunuchs, or those with dual sexual organs—provided that the three paths [of the body, speech, and mind] are all grave—the rest, such as praising, touching, or emitting impurity, are all merely the preliminary stages (*upāya*) of this precept and constitute minor offenses (*laghu-pāpaka*). Thus, the second stage below the Bodhisattva level clarifies what is appropriate. And...
Conversely, the third section below concludes this matter: all that is prohibited herein should not be done, for to do so constitutes an offense; thus it is concluded that they "should not be done.

The fourth is the precept against false speech. "False" is a term for that which is unreal. To deceive ordinary people and delude the sages, causing them to become confused and lost—this is what is meant by falsehood.

The reason the mind incurs an offense against this precept is that it is a violation common to all seven groups of practitioners; it is regulated by both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna, and its similarities and differences with those of the Śrāvakas are roughly the same as previously described.
If a disciple of the Buddha personally speaks falsely, teaches others to speak falsely, uses expedient means to speak falsely, or provides the causes and conditions for speaking falsely—

If a Bodhisattva engages in the practice of lying and the karma of lying— such as claiming to have seen what was not seen or claiming not to have seen what was seen— and while their own body and mind are characterized by such mental and physical falsehood,
they nevertheless constantly give rise to right speech and right view, and further cause all sentient beings to give rise to right speech and right view,
yet instead further incite all sentient beings to engage in wrong speech, wrong views, and wrong karma, this constitutes a *pārājika* offense for the Bodhisattva.
Offense.

Regarding the three stages of the introductory matter, the middle three should not be separated; the first three phrases clarify the matters such as false speech, while the latter three phrases clarify the completion of the karmic action.
By citing minor cases to illustrate major ones, "false speech" refers to claiming to have attained the state of a superior person (*uttarimanussa*).

Regarding teaching others: it refers to teaching and explaining, or teaching oneself while speaking to others, through the expedient means of false speech—such as when bees all come to a tree smeared with honey.
This precept is completed as a grave offense (*sthūlātyaya*) when five conditions are met: first, a sentient being; second, the perception of that being as such;
third, a deceptive intent; fourth, the utterance of the grave matter; and fifth, the listener’s comprehension. As for "first, a sentient being," it means:
Regarding the first three categories of objects and the superior category of objects: if one utters a lie toward one's parents, teachers, or the Sangha, it constitutes a grave offense (*pārājika*).

Regarding [lying to] the Buddhas and noble ones (*ārya*), there are two interpretations: first, some say it falls within the category of grave offenses; second, others say that because such a person is not deluded and possesses supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*) capable of shielding others so they do not hear, one commits only a minor defilement (*laghu-mala*). Furthermore, among noble ones, there are those who are "great" and those who possess the power of knowing the minds of others (*paracitta-jñāna*).

Regarding those for whom the wise do not incur [this offense], following the majority of precedents involving Arhats and those above the stage of "practice through understanding" (adhimukti-caryā), it was previously stated that the gravity of the transgression is lighter than this.
Whether one attains the knowledge of others' minds (paracitta-jñāna) or does not, the precedents are all identical in being heavy.

Regarding the middle-grade objects—humans, devas, and so forth—the gravity is exactly the same; this is precisely the limit that obstructs the path for both delusion and understanding. As for the lower-grade objects, there are four [cases].

Regarding the destinies (*gati*) and so forth, some say that [the offenses] are equally grave; now we explain that they are light defilements (*āpatti*). There are two types of perception regarding sentient beings:

those who exist, those who may exist, and those toward whom one has doubt or a distorted view; in general, these are similar to what was stated previously. Regarding false speech (*mṛṣāvāda*), it is said that the mind applies universally to this.
Even if one says, "I did not hear this, but he heard it," it is likewise grave; now we explain that it is not grave because there was no intent toward him. Third is the mind of deception.

If this master of the house flees from danger or acts out of overweening pride (*adhimāna*), he commits no offense. The *Bodhisattvabhūmi* states that for a bodhisattva, "savoring meditative concentration" (*dhyānāsvāda*) is called a defiled offense;
one should know that for a bodhisattva to give rise to overweening pride is likewise a minor transgression (*laghu-āpatti*). Regarding the dispatching of a messenger, there are two interpretations:
first, it is said that instructing another to say, "I am a holy person," is also a grave offense, for a man without jade or precious stones cannot speak [of such things].

First, regarding the value [of one's realization]: if others praise and describe one’s own path as superior to other paths, teaching them that this path is holy, yet fame and profit do not enter [one’s heart], then one’s non-attachment is not considered weighty.

Second, the holy Dharma is profound and subtle; its realization resides within oneself. It must necessarily be spoken by oneself to be considered weighty; speaking of it based on another’s account is deemed light.
Fourth, the "weighty requisites" refers to personally realizing and seeing with one’s own eyes; if one speaks of having attained the four fruits of the spiritual life, [it is weighty].

Regarding the ten stages (*bhūmi*), the eight dhyānas, and the supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), if one says that seeing devas, nāgas, ghosts, or spirits constitutes a grave offense involving all [factors], yet claims that attaining the stage of nature (*gotrabhūmi*) is light—first, it is said that since these are mundane dharmas, the defilement is light;

fifth, regarding the time of the offense and the number of people involved when the person understands and the offense is established, there are two interpretations: first, according to the person; second, according to the words. Since this precept has already been established...

Regarding the principle of restraining vocal karma, it should logically follow that speech constitutes an obstruction or harm; therefore, the precept against minor lying toward a person must necessarily apply both to the person and to the speech.

Furthermore, if one commits an offense through predominant afflictions (*kleśa*), it results in the loss of the vow; it is further stated that this applies only when one commits a transgression of essential nature (*prakṛti-sāvadya*).

Moreover, if the meaning is not understood face-to-face, one first incurs the offense of preliminary effort (*prayoga*); subsequently, if one reflects on the previous words and suddenly understands them, [the full offense is incurred].
This refers to the destruction of light fetters and the gravity of the ten grave offenses, all of which possess causes and conditions. For now, I shall explain the four grave offenses;

the others may be understood by analogy. To speak directly is called "utterance" (*vacana*); to proclaim and relate is called "speech" (*vākya*). To discourse so as to clarify and manifest, being able to demonstrate both principle and phenomena, is what is termed "speech."
○ The fifth precept: Selling Alcohol. "Selling" (酤) is a term for trade and commerce; "alcohol" is the commodity being traded.
There are many kinds of commodities, yet alcohol is the medicine of ignorance that causes people to become deluded. The essence of a Mahāsattva is to bestow wisdom upon others;
to give people the medicine of ignorance is not the conduct of a Bodhisattva. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* clarifies that there are three types of alcohol.

The fifteenth [offense] is included among the ten grave prohibitions for Bodhisattvas because it constitutes a failure in the means of restraint. It is a transgression common to the seven classes of followers, and it is regulated by both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna.

Regarding the similarities and differences between the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna: [the prohibition against] selling is common to both, yet it is grave for a Bodhisattva because they must benefit sentient beings, whereas for a Śrāvaka it is merely prohibited from being done.
To engage in the sale of goods constitutes a violation of the third category (the *sthūlātyaya*) in the case of the latter.
Regarding the prohibition against selling [forbidden items], if a Bodhisattva enters a brothel or sells meat, they commit a minor offense (*āpatti*);
this is because such acts involve summoning and attracting [customers] in a manner that cannot be compared to the sale of alcohol.
If a Buddha’s disciple sells alcohol themselves, teaches others to sell alcohol, or engages in the causes, conditions, methods, or practices of selling alcohol;
Regarding the liquor trade, one must not sell any kind of intoxicant, for such liquor is a cause and condition for the arising of transgressions.

Since a bodhisattva should instead give rise to the wisdom of clarity and penetration in all sentient beings, to instead further give rise to the minds of delusion and inversion in them constitutes a *pārājika* offense for that bodhisattva.
The phrasing is the same as before. Regarding the "seller" seeking profit: teaching others means causing people to sell wine for one's own sake; this is also equivalent [to selling it oneself].
Teaching others to sell on their own constitutes a lighter offense than selling it oneself. The four-line verse clarifying the completion of the karmic action follows below.
As for "action," it refers to the method of operation; this is the preparatory method (upāya) for selling wine. As for "conditions" (pratyaya), there are five requirements, the first of which is...
1. Sentient beings; 2. the perception of them as sentient beings; 3. seeking profit through selling; 4. genuine alcohol; 5. bestowing it upon another sentient being.

Regarding "sentient beings," this refers to the three aforementioned objects. If they are of superior grade and lack intoxication or confusion, the offense is light; if they are intoxicated or confused, it is heavy.

Objects of the middle grade refer to humans and devas, who are precisely those for whom the rule was established, and thus the offense is heavy. Objects of the inferior grade are the four realms of existence (*gati*); because their capacity for the path is weak, the offense is light.

If one sells [alcohol] to sentient beings with minor offenses, and harbors thoughts of its existence, doubts regarding its existence, or perverse views—as previously described—the offense is grave even if there is a separation of mind.
Selling it for the sake of profit is also grave, because of the desire to sell much. "True wine" refers to that which can intoxicate and delude people;
although medicinal wine may rarely cause intoxication at first, selling it is not an offense, as it does not delude people. One interpretation says: wait.

When drinking, the gravity of the offense is determined according to the number of people present. If a child comes to purchase [wine] and they ultimately do not drink it, with whom is the grave offense incurred?
The sixth [section] explains the precept regarding the censure of the fourfold assembly. This is a name for discussing the Path; "fourfold assembly" refers to those of the same Dharma.

The fourfold assembly’s transgressions consist of the seven reversals and the ten grave offenses. First, because they suppress and disparage others; second, because they damage the True Dharma, one incurs sin.
These precepts are violated by all seven groups of practitioners and are regulated by both Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna.

For a Bodhisattva, whose mind is intent on concealing evil and extolling goodness, the offense is particularly grave. "Superior" refers to the second category, "middling" to the third category, and "inferior" to the fourth.
This seventh category concerns the Śrāvaka teachings; such is the difference between them and those of the Bodhisattva.

If a son of the Buddha—whether a lay or ordained Bodhisattva, a Bhikṣu, or a Bhikṣuṇī—speaks of the transgressions of others, instructing people to speak of their faults, including the causes of those faults, the conditions for those faults, the nature of those faults, and the karmic actions of those faults, and if another Bodhisattva hears this...
If a Bodhisattva, toward those who revile the Buddha-dharma— namely, evil persons and those of the two vehicles who speak what is neither Dharma nor Vinaya within the Buddha-dharma—
should instead constantly give rise to a mind of loving-kindness and teach these evil people so as to cause them to produce wholesome faith in the Mahāyāna,
yet the Bodhisattva conversely speaks of the faults and transgressions within the Buddha-dharma himself, this constitutes a *pārājika* offense for that Bodhisattva.

The phrasing is the same as before. This precept is completed as a grave offense (*sthūlātyaya*) when six conditions are present: first, a sentient being; second, the perception of that being as a sentient being; third, the intention to speak of their fault;
fourth, the specific fault spoken of; fifth, the person to whom it is spoken; and sixth, the understanding by that person.

Regarding the first condition, "a sentient being," this refers to objects of superior or middling capacity; it is considered grave only when the person possesses the Bodhisattva precepts, as they would otherwise cause obstruction.

Because his superior karma [is such that] he lacks the bodhisattva precepts and possesses only the śrāvaka precepts, and because he has fallen into an inferior state where there are both those with precepts and those without precepts, he commits light defilements (*mṛdula-āpatti*).
This precept restrains him concurrently because it obstructs the conditions for his practice. As the text says:

"The lay bodhisattva refers to the pure-faith male and female devotees (*upāsaka* and *upāsikā*); the renunciant bodhisattva refers to those who possess the ten precepts or the full precepts; furthermore, it refers to bhikṣus."

Regarding the bhikṣuṇī: first, it is said that she is merely a bodhisattva who has left the household life through the Way and possesses the full precepts; second, it is said that she is a śrāvaka nun.

If one speaks of this person’s grave transgression, one also commits a grave offense, because even though she is a superior practitioner of the Dharma, she nonetheless causes harm to the profound Dharma.

Regarding the perception of sentient beings, there are three cases—certainly perceiving them as such, perceiving them with doubt, or perceiving them erroneously—the general meaning of which is the same as before.
Regarding the third point, speaking of faults, there are two types: first, the intention to cause the other person to lose reputation, profit, or honor;
second, the intention to punish them by causing them to be bound or imprisoned. These two states of mind constitute the essential factor (*karmavastu*);

one will certainly incur this offense if one speaks of faults with such intent. However, if one speaks out of a motive to encourage reform or if one speaks because one has been formally appointed to do so, there is no offense. Fourth... [the text ends here].

Regarding the statement that the names of those who have committed the seven heinous offenses (*saptānantarya*) or the ten grave transgressions (*daśa-guru-apatti*) are mentioned here as being subject to this precept:
this is the primary regulation. If one speaks of disciplinary punishment, that refers to the forty-eighth precept concerning the violation of the Dharma.

If one speaks of shedding the blood of a Buddha or causing a schism in the Sangha, these are based on the original regulations of the Vinaya-piṭaka; to speak of such matters before the Sangha is slanderous, for it is rare for such acts as shedding blood to actually occur.
If one treats this precept lightly and explains it to those who lack discipline, one should incur a grave offense;
yet, if one applies the name "grave" to what is actually grave, while applying the name "light" to what is actually grave according to its meaning, this is called losing the correct meaning.

However, if both the mind and the matter are grave, they are equally considered a grave offense. This is called a perversion of the name. As for a perversion of the matter, if one regards what is actually light as grave, then...

When a grave offense is truly grave, it is called light only if the mind considers it light; thus, the gravity of the sin corresponds to the gravity of the intention. Regarding the sending of a letter or dispatching a messenger:
one view holds that this is equally grave, while another holds that the sin is light. Furthermore, if one commits the seven reversals or the ten grave offenses, the recipient loses their precepts;

once the precepts are lost, the confession is valid. However, if one commits only a minor stain (*āpatti*), it is said that one may confess before five persons—provided they are of the superior or middle grade—and there is no [qualifying] absence.
Regarding the Bodhisattva precepts, because the offense of violating the profound dharma was previously explained as being grave, speaking of it to an inferior object is entirely light.

As for "insulting and disparaging," the text states that when a Bodhisattva hears non-Buddhists or followers of the Two Vehicles speak of faults in the Buddha-dharma, they ought to teach and transform them with compassion;
yet if one instead speaks of those very faults oneself, this constitutes a severe insult and disparagement toward that person. Sixth, the preceding person.

Having understood what was said regarding the matter of verbal karma, the offense is now established at this time. As for the number of offenses established, one view holds that it follows the person, while another view holds that it follows the verbal karma.
○ Seventh, the precept against praising oneself and disparaging others: "Praising oneself" means extolling one's own merits; "disparaging others" means...

To revile the faults and evils of others involves two matters; therefore, it is a grave offense for a Bodhisattva. One should maintain rectitude toward others while drawing the crookedness toward oneself;
how then can one raise up oneself to disparage others? Thus, this constitutes an offense. All seven assemblies commit this equally, as it is prohibited by both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna.

However, because the Bodhisattva takes the benefit and peace of others as their primary aim, the offense for praising or disparaging [others] is more severe than that of a Śrāvaka, who does not concern himself with others; thus, the Śrāvaka incurs the offense only when disparaging others.
The third section on self-praise constitutes an offense of the seventh category.
If a Buddha’s disciple praises themselves and disparages others, or teaches others to praise themselves and disparage others— whether through the cause of disparaging others,

the condition of disparaging others, the method of disparaging others, or the action of disparaging others— the Bodhisattva should instead undergo all the abuse, insults, and evil directed toward all sentient beings.
To take for oneself what belongs to others, to give one's own good deeds to others, or to proclaim one's own virtues while concealing the good deeds of others so that they suffer disgrace—
this constitutes a *pārājika* offense for a bodhisattva.
The phrasing is the same as before. This precept is completed as a grave offense (*sthūlātyaya*) when five conditions are met:

first, a sentient being; second, the perception of that being as such; third, the intention to praise or disparage; fourth, the expression of praise or disparagement; and fifth, the listener’s comprehension. Regarding the first condition, "a sentient being":

one view holds that disparaging superior or middling objects constitutes a grave offense, while disparaging inferior objects constitutes a light offense. Another view holds that [disparaging] both superior and middling objects [constitutes a grave offense].
