Regarding the matters: (1) performing prostrations and welcoming [the guest] by providing bedding and other requisites for the monks; (2) assigning monks in order, speaking words such as "I sell my own body to provide for you," which serve as an illustrative expression.
Regarding the third point, "not acting improperly": within the section on what is improper, only the instance of assigning monks out of order is cited;
this refers to the latter case while simultaneously including the former. If one does not share the goods with the monks, one does not perform the welcoming.

This same regulation applies here as well: if one knows that it is one’s turn in the monastic order (*saṃghakrama*) to reach a certain person, yet they do not appoint them and instead seize [the position], one commits only a minor offense (*laghuka-pāyattika*), because at the time of the appointment there may still be someone arriving from outside the boundary who has not yet been definitively assigned a share.

If, after the appointment is completed, one seizes it and gives it to another, and the other person knows this, then both the appointer and the appointed are guilty of the preliminary stage of theft (*steya-prayoga*). Subsequently—
If one receives food from a donor's house and accepts five *kārsāpaṇas* into one's hand, each constitutes a grave offense, no different from keeping livestock;
or, this refers to the precept against bypassing the order of monks, for there are six ways of bypassing the order of monks as explained in the Vinaya.

○ Twenty-seventh: The Precept Against Accepting Individual Invitations. To accept individual invitations separately means that the donor does not invite the Sangha of the ten directions, thereby causing the donor to lose the merit of an impartial mind and the Sangha of the ten directions to lose their regular share of offerings;

therefore, this is prescribed as a shared offense for the five groups of renunciants. The two groups of householders do not have this specific benefit [of communal distribution], and thus it was not prescribed for them. It applies to both Mahayana and Hinayana.
First interpretation: In the Sangha of Bodhisattvas, all offerings and alms for general assemblies must be discontinued if there is a separate invitation.

However, if one is invited to receive precepts or preach the Dharma, or if one perceives through direct observation (*jñāna*) or inferential knowledge (*anumāna*) that this person is free from the notion of self (*anātman*), then one does not cultivate merit [for oneself].
Such cases are not prohibited. Second interpretation: From four people upwards, if there is at least one member of the Sangha present, it is not an offense; if there is none at all, it is.
The meaning of the text of this precept seems to follow the previous interpretation:
"If a disciple of the Buddha, he must not under any circumstances accept special invitations for offerings and take them for himself; for such offerings belong to the Sangha of the ten directions.
To accept a special invitation is to take the property of the Sangha of the ten directions for oneself, as well as [to misappropriate] that which belongs among the eight fields of merit."
To take for one's own use the property of the Buddhas, the sages, individual teachers, parents, or the sick constitutes a minor offense (laghu-āpatti).

This concludes the third section of the introduction, which initially indicates what is improper; hereafter follows the second part, the explanation of the meaning of that impropriety, concerning the donor.
One should know that the method for cultivating merit ought to be vast and universal; the benefit of giving fundamentally pervades the ten directions.

Because you receive it individually, the ten directions cannot be said to be remote, and thus there is no principle of "seizing" from the ten directions. Therefore, one should not regard these three [types of recipients] as being inferior to the eight fields of merit (*aṣṭa-puṇyakṣetra*).

These three should not be considered distinct from the eight fields of merit, as they possess the same quality of being worthy of offerings as the Saṃgha in its sequential order (*saṃghānupūrvī*), just like the Buddha’s manifested traces (*nirmāṇakāya*).
The eight fields of merit for the Sangha and others are: first, the Buddha; second, noble beings (āryas); third, the preceptor (upādhyāya); fourth, the instructor (ācārya);

fifth, the Sangha; sixth, one’s father; seventh, one’s mother; and eighth, the sick. Now, within the Tripiṭaka, it is said that the Buddha constantly accepts individual invitations without being considered to have committed an offense.
This is because the Buddha is the supreme field of merit, and his merit does not diminish through such impartiality of mind. Second, in this land, there is only...
One Buddha does not possess the quality of supplanting the significance of another Buddha.
○ The twenty-eighth precept concerning the separate invitation of monks distinguishes between who is a field of merit and who is not;

as stated in the "Chapter on King Guṇa" of the Mahāvaipulya Sūtra, one should know that such a mind is narrow and inferior, and it loses the mind of equanimity. All seven classes of followers commit this offense equally.

In the Hīnayāna, the path is not entirely shared by monastics and laypeople. Regarding the Bodhisattva’s invitation of the Sangha for a vegetarian feast: First interpretation: One must never invite separately; one should instead invite according to the order of the Sangha.

If one invites a single person [out of order], one commits an offense. Second interpretation: At a single meal site, regardless of the number of people, if one merely invites one person according to the Sangha order, there is no offense.
If there is no one at all [in the order], then it is regulated that if one invites everyone [without regard for order], [there is no fault].
Furthermore, the meaning of the text seems to be as explained previously.

If, O Sons of the Buddha—whether they be ordained bodhisattvas, lay bodhisattvas, or any donors (dānapati)—should wish to invite the Sangha as a field of merit to fulfill a vow, they should go to the monks' quarters and inquire of the administrative officer (vaiyāvṛtyakara), saying: "I now wish to invite the Sangha to fulfill a vow."
The attendant replied: "Those who invite according to the sequence of the assembly shall obtain the noble and holy Sangha of the ten directions.

It is better for a worldly person to invite one ordinary monk according to the sequence of the assembly than to separately invite five hundred Arhats or Bodhisattvas. To separately invite monks is the practice of external paths;
the Seven Buddhas had no such practice of separate invitations. This does not accord with the Way of Filial Piety; if one intentionally invites monks separately, one commits an offense."
Minor Taints (Kṣudra-āpatti). Section Three: The Three Stages. First, the indication of the response; second, the explanation of the meaning of the response.

It clarifies that although one may receive an invitation from ordinary monks (*prthagjana-bhikṣu*), there is a superior and specific invitation for the Holy Sangha (*ārya-saṃgha*). Thus it is said: "Five hundred Arhats are not equal to one ordinary monk."

The Sangha here is discussed from the perspective of the mind, without regard for the field [of merit]. If one makes separate invitations, those belonging to the lower three [vehicles] should not be included;
they should not be treated like non-Buddhists who follow different teachings, as this would contradict the Way of Filial Piety.

As for the Seven Buddhas, they all appeared within this land through their transformations, and their traces were active within the last hundred kalpas; since they were all seen by those in the Heaven of Long Life (*Āyuṣmat*), seven are frequently cited.
The Buddha, desiring to make the meaning clear for those who believe, testified that ninety kalpas ago there was a Buddha named Vipaśyin, also called Vīra.
During the intervening kalpas, there were no Buddhas until the thirty-first kalpa, when two Buddhas appeared:
the first named Śikhin and the second named Viśvabhū, also called Subhi. This is the ninth [kalpa] of the ninety.
One kalpa is named the Bhadrakalpa (Auspicious Kalpa), during which one thousand Buddhas are destined to appear; four have already passed:
first, Krakucchanda; second, Kanakamuni; third, Kāśyapa; and fourth, Śākyamuni.
○ Regarding the twenty-ninth precept on wrong livelihood (*mithyājīva*): The *Mahā-śāstra* states that when a greedy mind gives rise to actions of body and speech, it is termed wrong livelihood.
The text enumerates seven examples; those who act similarly all commit this offense and deviate from pure livelihood.
If a Buddha’s disciple, out of an evil mind and for the sake of profit, sells the sexual favors of men or women; prepares food with their own hands, grinds or husks grain themselves;
practices physiognomy on men and women, interprets dreams as auspicious or inauspicious, or determines whether a child will be male or female;

or employs incantations, technical skills, medical treatments, and medicinal formulas to compound hundreds or thousands of kinds of poisons, including snake venom, artificial gold and silver poisons, and *gū* (poisonous fungi).
If one lacks any heart of compassion or filial piety, and intentionally commits such acts, one incurs a minor offense (light impurity).
The introductory matter has three stages: first, regarding the malicious intent for profit, which involves discerning the occasion to benefit sentient beings; second, listing the seven matters;
third, citing the improper conduct to conclude the fault—namely, because of a lack of compassion, one commits the wrong livelihood of a Śrāvaka, which consists of four types of sustenance.
Looking upward and looking downward, these four; herein, five matters pertain to the preceding four types of sustenance: first, trafficking in female beauty; second, preparing food for oneself;
third, divining auspicious and inauspicious signs—whereby laypeople live according to such omens without offense, whereas for those on the Path this is strictly prohibited;
fourth, incantations and sorcery; fifth, the arts and crafts; sixth, the methods of healing and medicine—these three.

In one's dealings with things, one must not encroach upon others, but live according to the Dharma. While those at home are not yet restrained, those who have left the household life must completely sever such ties.

If one practices medicine purely, harboring no expectations for gain, there is no offense; likewise, the compounding of medicines is permitted for renunciants. However, it is a transgression to compound poisons that kill people.

○ The thirtieth precept: Not honoring auspicious times. The three fasting days (*trayāṇām upavāsānām*) and the six fasting days (*ṣaḍ upavāsāḥ*) are all days upon which spirits and deities gain power;

on these days, one should cultivate merit and virtue more than on other days. If, during such auspicious times, one is negligent or disrespectful and further commits an offense, the guilt shall be determined according to the specific transgression and the relevant category of the precepts. On such times and such days, one must not remain ignorant; [if so], an additional offense is incurred.
Regarding the first point on the precepts: it is said that all seven groups of practitioners are equally bound by the rules and should observe them at all times. Regarding the second point:

it is said that they are only bound [by the rules] when at home during the three long fasting months and the six fasting days; originally, both laypeople and monastics observe the fast for as long as they live, regardless of specific seasons or dates.
If a disciple of the Buddha, out of an evil mind, slanders the Triple Gem themselves while falsely appearing to be close to them;
if they speak of emptiness with their mouth but act within the realm of existence; if they manage affairs for laypeople, acting as an intermediary between men and women for sexual intercourse;

if they create various bonds and attachments; and if on the six days of fasting or during the three long months of fasting, they commit killing, robbery, or violate the precepts—[they shall be guilty].
Regarding the precepts, one incurs a minor offense (light defilement).

In the introductory section, there are three stages: first, a general enumeration of the violations of the precepts; second, that whatever is transgressed constitutes a discrepancy between words and deeds, a deviation from the true and correct, and a slander against the Triple Gem;
third, regarding the six days of fasting (the *ṣaḍ-upoṣadha*), this refers to the two occasions of reverence. These are the six... [text ends].

Regarding the three types of fasts, such as the three long fasts (*tridīrgha-upavāsa*), the act of killing sentient beings follows next. Thirdly, we again cite the transgressions that constitute the commission of offenses.
Regarding killing and stealing, we briefly cite the first two grave violations of the fast, namely eating at improper times (*akālabhojana*) and so forth. The *Upāsaka-śīla-sūtra* states:
"On the six days of the fast (*ṣaḍupavāsa-dina*) and during the three months of the fast, one should receive the eight precepts and observe the fast; a lay bodhisattva should practice this."
Matters.
These ten precepts should be studied and upheld with a reverent heart, as explained in detail in the "Chapter on the Precepts" (*Śīlaskandhaka*).
This concludes the third section on these ten precepts.

○ The thirty-first precept: Not redeeming [images]. To see that images of Buddhas or Bodhisattvas are being sold and not to redeem them—this is an extreme form of humiliation and is not the conduct of a Mahāsattva.
One should redeem them according to one’s capacity; failure to do so constitutes an offense.

Therefore, this is prescribed as a shared offense for all seven assemblies, though the gravity of the transgression differs between the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna. A Bodhisattva must redeem them. As for a Śrāvaka, if he sees his father...
The Mother does not redeem [them]; this constitutes an offense of the seventh category (*saptama-pārājika*). Regarding the sutras and images, there is no specific prohibition.

The Buddha said: "O Son of the Buddha, after my parinirvāṇa, in this evil age, if you see non-Buddhists, various wicked people, bandits, or thieves selling images of the Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, or one's parents;
or if you see them selling the sutras and vinaya, or trafficking in bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs..."
If a bhikṣuṇī sells a person who has generated the bodhicitta— a practitioner of the Bodhisattva path— or if such a person is conscripted by the government as a laborer or made a slave to anyone,
the Bodhisattva, having seen this situation, should give rise to a mind of compassion and employ skillful means to rescue and protect them.
They should teach and transform people everywhere to obtain goods to redeem the images of Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, as well as bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs who have generated the bodhicitta.
If one does not redeem any of the sutras or vinayas, one commits a minor offense (light defilement).
Regarding the introductory matter, there are three points: first, the person who is able to sell them refers to a bandit who sells [images];

these are the forms of Buddhas and Bodhisattvas. Because they have parents, they possess great compassion; therefore, according to the third section of the Bodhisattva precepts, one ought to rescue them.

This is for the purpose of redemption. ○ The thirty-second precept: The Prohibition Against Harming Sentient Beings. This consists of six matters; it is established because harming sentient beings violates compassion and must be prevented from afar.
It is a transgression for all seven classes of practitioners, and is regulated by both the Mahayana and Hinayana.
If a Buddha’s disciple sells swords, staves, bows, or arrows; uses light scales or small measures; uses official authority or power to seize the property of others;
harms sentient beings by binding them; or raises cats, raccoons, pigs, and dogs to ruin successful undertakings—if they do any of these intentionally, they commit a minor offense.

The introductory section enumerates six matters: first, selling implements for killing; second, keeping light scales and small measures, as well as short lengths of measuring rods—these follow the same principle;
third, seeking and obtaining money through official influence; fourth, harming others with a malicious intent or binding them;
fifth, destroying successful undertakings; sixth, raising cats and wildcats. These six things all involve harm.
One should not keep items that cause injury or damage.

○ The thirty-third precept concerns improper mental activity (*vitarka-vicāra*). Whatever actions one undertakes, if they are not right action and if one's thoughts and mental observations disturb the True Path, this precept is established.
It is a violation for both the Great and Small Vehicles; however, the seven groups of practitioners do not all incur the offense in the same way.
If a disciple of the Buddha, out of a malicious mind, observes all men and women fighting, or armies, generals, and bandits engaged in combat,
they must not listen to the sounds of conchs, drums, horns, lutes, harps, zithers, flutes, *konghou* lutes, singing, shouting, or the music of courtesans.
They must not play at gambling games, *weiqi*, *bolasai*, *danyi*, *liubo*, ball games, stone-throwing, or any such diversions.
One must not engage in divination using pitch-pot games, pulling ropes, the eight paths, the city walls, fingernails, mirrors, milfoil stalks, willow branches, alms bowls, or skulls;
one must not act as a thief or a messenger. If one does so intentionally, one commits a minor offense (light defilement).
Preface: Three matters; first, the prohibition against viewing with an evil mind; second, discerning the opportunity; third, the two categories of matters; third, the general conclusion.

The general outline of the categorized matters consists of five points: First, regarding the two matters of not being permitted to view [images], this regulation applies equally to both monastics and laypeople.
Second, if for one’s own amusement, neither monastics nor laypeople may create or listen to [such things]; however, if it is for the purpose of making offerings, [it is permitted]. Third...
The Jewel Path is opened equally for both monastics and laypeople. Third, regarding the eight matters, one must not engage in frivolous games;
fourth, regarding the six matters, one must not practice divination for profit—these are rules prescribed for both monastics and laity alike. Fifth, regarding diplomatic missions.

○ Thirty-fourth: Briefly considering the precepts of the Hīnayāna, because they deviate from what one has originally practiced, it is ordained that the seven classes of followers commit this offense equally;

however, as the practices of the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna differ, this is an offense not shared between them. If one intends to turn away from the Mahāyāna toward the Hīnayāna, the offense occurs when the mental resolve is not yet finalized (the eighth offense).
If the resolve to turn away from the Mahāyāna toward the Hīnayāna is finalized, one loses the precepts; this is explained among the tenth category of grave offenses.

That which is regulated by these precepts does not seek to turn away from the Great [Vehicle] or to claim the Small Vehicle as easy to practice; rather, one desires first to sever the fetters and subsequently attain birth through transformation.

If a disciple of the Buddha protects and upholds the prohibitive precepts, whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, they should recite these precepts during the six periods of day and night.
One should be like a diamond, like one wearing a belt while carrying a life-preserving float intending to cross the great ocean, or like a bhikṣu bound by grass.
One should constantly give rise to wholesome faith in the Mahāyāna, knowing for oneself: "I am a Buddha-to-be, while the Buddhas are Buddhas already accomplished.

One should resolve upon Bodhicitta, never letting it depart from the mind even for a single thought-moment. If one gives rise to a single thought of the Two Vehicles or of non-Buddhists, one commits a minor transgression.
Regarding the offense:
the introductory matter has two parts. First, concerning the response, there is a brief presentation of three points for those who respond by contemplating the Mahāyāna:

first, guarding the Mahāyāna precepts, which generally presents two analogies—first, the diamond, taken in the sense of firmness; second, the life-preserving raft, as in the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*. Second, the exit via the binding with grass.
Through the *Nidāna-sūtra*, one gives rise to Mahāyāna faith in two ways and awakens the Mahāyāna mind in three ways.

If the latter two [stages] arise, one must not, even for a single thought-moment, give rise to the notion of self-deliverance. As for "outsiders" (*bāhya*), this refers to those of the Two Vehicles (*dvayayāna*) as being outsiders;
however, if they have expediently entered these paths for the sake of transformation, they are not subject to such restrictions.

○ The thirty-fifth precept against failing to make vows: A bodhisattva should constantly vow to seek superior matters and direct the mind toward wholesome objects, for by means of this, future goals will surely be accomplished;
if one does not make vows to seek what is good, it is difficult to achieve success.

Therefore, this is established as a rule for all seven classes of followers, regardless of whether they follow the Mahāyāna or Hīnayāna, because although their specific practices differ, the requirement is the same.

If a Buddha’s disciple constantly aspires to make all vows, they should be filial toward their parents and respectful toward their teachers, monks, and the Triple Gem; they should vow to obtain a good teacher, fellow students,

and virtuous spiritual friends who will constantly instruct them in the Mahāyāna sūtras and vinaya— the ten stages of setting forth, the ten stages of nurturing, the ten adamantine stages, and the ten bhūmis—
so that they may achieve understanding and practice according to the Dharma, firmly upholding the Buddha’s precepts even at the cost of their own bodies and lives.
This thought should not leave the mind for even a single moment; if any bodhisattva does not make this vow, they commit a minor offense.

Regarding the sequence of matters, there are three parts: first, the essence of the vow; second, what should be done; third, what should not be done. First, the essence of the vow consists of ten points:
(1) to vow to be filial toward one's parents, teachers, and monks; (2) to vow to obtain a good teacher; (3) to vow to obtain superior friends and fellow students.
Fourth, may you teach me the Mahāyāna Vinaya; fifth, may you explain the ten stages of departure (*daśa-prasthāna*); sixth, may you explain the ten stages of nourishment (*daśa-poṣaṇa*);
seventh, may you explain the ten adamantine stages (*daśa-vajra*); eighth, may you explain the ten stages (*daśa-bhūmi*); ninth, may you practice according to the Dharma;
tenth, may you firmly uphold the Buddha’s precepts. It is better to abandon the lower [stages]; second, one should give rise to this mind; third, suffering all that is inferior.
One should not, one should not fail to give rise to this mind.
○ Thirty-sixth: The Precept Against Not Making Vows. A vow is a firm and resolute heart’s resolve; it is the courageous intent within one’s aspirations.
If the initial impulse of the mind is weak, one must guard and maintain it. If one does not give rise to the resolve or apply the mind, transgression will arise.

Regarding the transgressions of the precepts established by the Buddha, although all seven groups of followers commit them equally, their application does not necessarily apply to everyone; thus, the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna are not shared, and the two vehicles do not establish prohibitions for those whose minds are easily guarded and maintained.
If a disciple of the Buddha, having made these ten great vows, upholds the Buddha’s prohibitive precepts, they should make this vow, saying: "I would rather [suffer] by means of this..."

One would rather cast one's body into a great pit of blazing, fierce fire or onto a mountain of knives than ever violate the sutras and vinaya of the Buddhas of the three periods of time by engaging in impure conduct with any woman.

Furthermore, he makes this vow: "I would rather have my body bound on all sides by a thousand layers of glowing iron mesh than, with a body that has broken the precepts, accept any clothing from a faithful donor."

Furthermore, he makes this vow: "I would rather swallow glowing iron balls and endure great, raging flames with these lips for hundreds of thousands of kalpas than ever, with a mouth that has broken the precepts, eat the food of a hundred flavors offered by a faithful donor.
He further makes this vow: "I would rather lie upon this body on a floor of great, raging flames, iron nets, and glowing iron than ever..."
One whose body has violated the precepts may receive from a faithful donor a hundred kinds of seats and couches;

yet they should further make this vow: "I would rather have this body endure three hundred spears piercing it for one kalpa or two kalpas than ever again, with a body that has violated the precepts, accept from a faithful donor the medicinal provisions of a hundred flavors."

Furthermore, he makes this vow: "I would rather cast this body into a cauldron of molten iron for hundreds of thousands of kalpas than ever again receive with a body of broken precepts the thousandfold offerings of houses, dwellings, gardens, and fields from faithful donors."

Furthermore, he makes this vow: "I would rather have this body smashed from head to foot with an iron hammer until it is like fine dust, than ever receive the respectful prostrations of a faithful donor with a body that has broken the precepts."

He further makes this vow: "I would rather have my two eyes gouged out by a hundred thousand heated iron swords and spears than ever look upon the beautiful forms of others with a mind that violates the precepts.
He further makes this vow: "I would rather have my faculty of hearing pierced by a hundred thousand iron awls for one kalpa or two kalpas..."
One does not listen to pleasant sounds with a mind of broken precepts.
Furthermore, one makes this vow: "I would rather have my nose cut off by a hundred thousand blades than ever, with a mind of broken precepts, greedily smell various fragrances."

He further makes this vow: "I would rather have my tongue severed by hundreds of thousands of sharp blades than ever, with a mind of broken precepts, eat the hundred flavors of pure food offered by others.
He further makes this vow: "I would rather have my body hacked and split apart by a sharp axe than ever, with a mind of broken precepts, harbor greed..."
One should wear fine garments.
Furthermore, one should make this vow: "May all sentient beings attain Buddhahood. If a Bodhisattva does not make this vow, they commit a minor offense.
The introductory matter has three parts: first, the initial phrase sets forth the exhortation to give rise to the ten vows, which should be vowed and maintained through the observance of precepts;
next, the final phrase concludes that failing to do so constitutes a transgression; and finally, the thirteen "furthermore" sections in between correctly clarify the essential substance of the vows.
○ The thirty-seventh precept: Prohibiting Traveling While Endangering One’s Life. Those who have begun the bodhisattva path are for the most part unsettled;

furthermore, a human body that is fit to serve as a vessel for the Way is difficult to obtain. If one travels carelessly, it may lead to premature death. When life is in peril, the consequences of such loss are grave.
Because of this lack of caution, this rule is established; all seven classes of followers commit an offense by violating it, and both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna traditions prohibit it equally.
If a Buddha’s disciple constantly observes the two periods for *dhūta* practice— meditating in winter and summer— and maintains the summer retreat (*varṣā*), they should always carry a tooth-stick,

cleansing powder, the three robes, a water jar, an alms bowl, a sitting mat, a mendicant’s staff, an incense burner, a water-strainer, a hand-towel, a small knife, a flint and steel, tweezers, a rope bed,
and copies of the Sūtras, Vinaya, and images of Buddhas and Bodhisattvas; thus does a Bodhisattva practice the *dhūta* austerities.
Whether traveling for a time or journeying for a hundred or a thousand *li*, these eighteen kinds of items must always accompany the person.

For a *dhūta* practitioner, during these two periods—from the fifteenth day of the first month to the fifteenth day of the third month, and from the fifteenth day of the eighth month to the fifteenth day of the tenth month—these eighteen kinds of items must always accompany the person. Just as...

Just as a bird has two wings, so too, on the days of the *poṣadha*, a newly initiated bodhisattva should regularly observe the *poṣadha* every half-month and recite the ten grave and forty-eight light precepts. When reciting the precepts, one should do so before images of the Buddhas and bodhisattvas.
Whether it is a single person observing the *poṣadha*, or two, three, or even up to a hundred thousand people, they should likewise recite them.
When one person recites and another listens, the reciter shall occupy a high seat while the listener remains on a lower seat; each shall don the nine-strip, seven-strip, or five-strip *kāṣāya*.
When observing the summer retreat (*varṣā*), one should likewise act in accordance with the Dharma in every respect.

When practicing the ascetic disciplines (*dhūta*), do not enter dangerous places, such as regions with wicked rulers, lands where the terrain is treacherous, or where the vegetation is dense and overgrown. Master.
Regarding the difficulties caused by tigers, wolves, water, fire, wind, bandits on the road, venomous snakes,
and all such perilous places, one must not enter them while practicing *dhūta* austerities or during the summer retreat (*varṣā*).
If one intentionally enters such dangerous places, one commits a minor offense (*duṣkṛta*).
The introductory matter has three layers. First, clarifying the appropriate conduct for traveling and staying constitutes the primary condition for the establishment of the precepts.

Furthermore, there are three initial points: first, clarifying traveling and staying; second, the eighteen items to be carried at all times; third, the two periods of *dhūta* practice. "Traveling" refers to the period of wandering.
During the two seasons of spring and autumn, one travels with moderation; thus, in transforming sentient beings, there is no hindrance or harm. Regarding the head... [text fragment].

There are twelve great treatises [on this]. Regarding food, there are five [practices]: first, not accepting special invitations; second, always begging for alms; third, not drinking liquids after midday;
fourth, eating in a single sitting; fifth, moderation in the amount of food. Regarding the dwelling place, there are five:

first, a forest hermitage (*āraṇyaka*); second, always sitting and never lying down; third, dwelling among tombs; fourth, sitting at the foot of a tree; fifth, [dwelling in an open, unsheltered space].

Regarding dwelling in the open air and the practice of wearing robes, there are two points: first, one should possess only the three robes; second, one should constantly wear the patched robe (*kaṣāya*).

Because wandering during the winter cold and summer heat causes much inconvenience and damage, this regulation was established. If one does not comply with this regulation, one commits a minor offense (*duṣkṛta*).

Some say that when a Bodhisattva makes a vow for the summer retreat (*varṣā*), it lasts five months or three months, from the latter half of the fifth month to the first half of the eighth month. As the text states:

At this time, one no longer practices *dhūta* austerities; furthermore, this is the limit for the summer retreat (*varṣā*). To wander about and expose oneself to hardships during this period is strictly prohibited.
Thirty-eighth:
The Precept on Violating the Order of Seniority. Because violating the proper order leads to a loss of decorum, this precept was established for the seven classes of followers.
The precepts for both major and minor offenses are equally established.
If, O sons of the Buddha, you sit according to the proper sequence of the Dharma, those who received the precepts first shall sit in front,
and those who received them later shall sit behind, regardless of whether they are senior or junior, monks or nuns, or even nobles, kings, or princes.
Eunuchs and slaves should all sit first according to the order of their prior reception of the precepts; those who received them later should sit in successive order.
Do not be like the deluded people of external paths, whether old or young, sitting without priority or sequence, following the manner of soldiers or slaves.
In my Buddha-dharma, those who came first sit first, and those who came later sit later; yet the Bodhisattva is one [in essence].
First, to sit out of the proper sequence is an offense of light impurity.

Regarding the three stages of the introductory ritual: first, one should follow the proper order; do not act like the heretics who sit in the lower [positions]. Second, one should not be improper; one must not disrupt the sequence.
Third, this concludes the meaning of what is appropriate and inappropriate within my Dharma. The sequential order for Śrāvakas is set forth in the Vinaya.

Regarding the rules for bedding and requisites in the various divisions, they are ranked according to the precepts. Even down to the duration of a *mahā-muhūrta*, all are designated as "senior" (*sthavira*).
This path is common to both monastics and laity, comprising nine groups: first, bhikṣus; second, bhikṣuṇīs; third, ṣaḍvarṣikā bhikṣuṇīs;
fourth, śrāmaṇeras; fifth, śrāmaṇerīs; sixth, male renunciants; seventh, female renunciants; eighth, upāsakas; and ninth, upāsikās. This is [the rule].
The nine assemblies have a fixed order that must not be confused, as explained in the Vinaya section. [Section] Thirty-nine:
Not Cultivating Merit and Wisdom. The two adornments of merit and wisdom are like the two wings of a bird;

they must not fail to be cultivated, for to neglect them is to deviate from the path of liberation. Therefore, it is prescribed that all seven assemblies incur this offense equally, whether following the Mahāyāna or Hīnayāna.

All together, Bodhisattvas should encompass all wholesome dharmas; they should practice the summer retreat (*varṣā*) as Śrāvakas do, and they should personally vow to cultivate meritorious deeds at other times without restriction.
If a son of the Buddha, he should constantly teach and transform all sentient beings, establishing monastic dwellings, mountain forests, gardens, and fields.

One should establish [this practice] at all places where Buddha-stūpas are built, during the winter and summer retreats for seated meditation, and at all sites for the practice of the Way; furthermore,
the Bodhisattva should expound the Mahāyāna sūtras and vinaya for the sake of all sentient beings on occasions such as illnesses,
national calamities, or threats from bandits, as well as on the day of the passing away of parents, siblings, upādhyāyas, or ācāryas, and during the forty-nine days following their death.
From the fifth week up to the seventh week, one should likewise preach this Mahāyāna sūtra and vinaya at all assemblies for the observance of fasts seeking merit,
during travels for livelihood, and when afflicted by great fires, swept away by great floods, or driven by black winds;
or when facing the perils of ships upon rivers and great oceans, or the dangers of rākṣasas— one should read, recite, and preach this sūtra and vinaya, and indeed all such [scriptures].
Those who suffer the retribution of the three evil realms, the eight difficulties, and the seven heinous offenses; those bound by handcuffs, fetters, and shackles;
and those with excessive desire, excessive anger, excessive ignorance, and many illnesses—all such persons should read, recite, expound, and explain this sutra and its vinaya.
If a newly initiated bodhisattva does not do so, they commit a minor offense.
The introductory section on the three stages of practice for cultivating merit—both performing it oneself and instructing others—briefly outlines seven matters:
first, monasteries; second, mountain forests; third, gardens; fourth, fields; fifth, stupas; sixth, places for winter and summer meditation and retreats;
and seventh, all sites for the practice of the Way. All such categories as these should be established; however, if one lacks the capacity, one need not do so.
Having committed an offense, the second point to be practiced by a bodhisattva is wisdom; this involves both practicing it oneself and teaching others.
The third point concerns the newly initiated student: raising the issue of faults and establishing that the failure to practice constitutes a loss.
These nine precepts should be studied and upheld with a reverent mind; they shall be explained in detail within the *Brahmacarya-vastu*.
Thus, the fourth section concludes these nine precepts, which shall be explained in detail within the *Brahmacarya-vastu*.
Fortieth: Regarding the discernment of those who receive the precepts, if they possess the mental aspiration to receive them, all such persons should be granted [the ordination].

If one were to reject them out of anger or malice, it would contradict the spirit of encouragement; therefore, this rule was established. For the two groups of renunciants (monks and nuns), the offense is the same.

As for others who lack a teacher, the rule has not yet been established. Whether Mahāyāna or Hīnayāna, if the precepts are incomplete, they are not shared in common. The Bodhisattva precepts fundamentally include all beings, whereas the Śrāvaka precepts do not. If permission were granted therein, it would be [incomplete].
Regret concerns whether an offense has been committed or not;

it does not concern what was not committed. If, O Sons of the Buddha, when bestowing the precepts upon others, you do not discriminate among any kings, princes, ministers, officials, bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, laymen, laywomen, male or female practitioners of lust, or even the eighteen Brahmā heavens and the six [heavens of desire]...

Desiring that devas, sons of heaven, those without sexual organs, those with dual organs, eunuchs, slaves, and all ghosts and spirits may all receive the precepts, one should instruct them so that the robes they wear are all of "ruined color" (kasāya) to correspond with the Way;
all dyed garments—even down to bedding—should be entirely of ruined colors, such as blue, yellow, red, black, or purple. As for the single robe worn upon the body...
All dyed garments, or whatever clothing people in all lands wear, a bhikṣu must differ from such secular attire.
When one wishes to receive the precepts, the teacher should ask: "In your present body, have you not committed the seven heinous offenses?
A Dharma-master of the Bodhisattva path must not confer the precepts upon one who has committed the seven heinous offenses in their present body. As for the seven heinous offenses:

If one commits any of the seven heinous offenses—shedding the blood of a Buddha, killing one's father, killing one's mother, killing one's preceptor (upādhyāya), killing one's teacher (ācārya), causing a schism in the Saṃgha that obstructs the turning of the Wheel of Dharma, or killing an arhat—one shall not receive the precepts in this present life. All other persons may fully receive the precepts.
Regarding the dharma for those who have left the household life: one does not prostrate to kings, nor does one prostrate to one's parents. Six.

If one does not respect one's parents nor reverently serve the spirits, yet merely understands the words of the Dharma Master; and if there are those who come from as far as a hundred or a thousand *li* seeking the Dharma,
yet the Bodhisattva Dharma Master, out of an evil mind or a hateful mind, does not immediately bestow upon them the precepts for all sentient beings—
this constitutes an offense of light defilement.

The introductory matters are threefold: first, that which should not be scrutinized; second, that which should be scrutinized, which has two aspects: (1) the physical form, which should be scrutinized as being improper;
and (2) the karmic obstructions, which must be scrutinized as being improper. Regarding robes, while *śrāvakas* use blue clay [stains], Bodhisattvas should likewise use them.
According to the intent of this text, it appears they need not necessarily possess all [the requisites], provided they differ from those of the laity.

If the colors are not distinct, it is called "in accordance with the Dharma. One interpretation states that both monastics and laypeople must wear dyed (ruined-color) robes when receiving the precepts;

another states that this is a rule for dyeing applicable equally to monastics and laypeople. The text says, "It differs from that of the laity"; one should know that an ordained Bodhisattva must necessarily use dyed colors.
This concludes the section on the rules for ordained monastics. The third part below cites improper conduct to demonstrate its faults.

The forty-first precept, concerning acting as a teacher for the sake of profit: Because there is no genuine understanding within while externally acting out of desire for fame and gain, one rashly and forcibly pretends to possess it, resulting in the fault of misleading others; therefore, this is established as a transgression for both groups of monastics.
It is not established as a minor offense for the three assemblies of novices, nor is it established for laypeople, as they lack the status of being formal teachers.

If a Buddha-son, when teaching others to arouse faith, acts as an instructing Dharma-master for another, he should, upon seeing one who wishes to receive the precepts, instruct them to request two masters: an Upādhyāya and an Ācārya. These two masters should ask:
"Do you have any of the seven obstructing offenses? If there are any of the seven obstructing offenses manifest in this present life, the masters should not confer the precepts upon them.
If one is free from the seven grave prohibitions (*saptāvaraṇa*), one may receive the precepts.

If one has violated the ten major precepts, one should be taught to repent before an image of the Buddha or a Bodhisattva, reciting the ten heavy and forty-eight light precepts during the six periods of the day and night.
With utmost sincerity, one should prostrate to the thousand Buddhas of the three periods; if one perceives an auspicious sign after one week, two weeks, or even longer...
In one year, one must see auspicious signs (*lakṣaṇa*). These auspicious signs include the Buddha coming to touch one’s head, seeing light, seeing flowers, or various other extraordinary phenomena;

upon seeing these, one’s transgressions are extinguished. If no auspicious signs appear, although one performs repentance, it is of no benefit. Such a person will not obtain the precepts in their present life, yet they may receive them with increased merit.
As for those who have violated the forty-eight minor precepts, if they perform face-to-face repentance (*pratideśanā*), their transgressions are then [extinguished].
The attainment of cessation is not the same as the seven prohibitions; thus, the teacher of instruction must understand each point within this Dharma thoroughly.

If one does not understand the Mahāyāna sūtras and vinayas—whether their gravity is light or heavy, or the characteristics of what is right and wrong—one will not understand the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), nor the nature of the habit-seed (*vāsanā-bīja*), the nature of nurturing (*paripuṣṭa-bīja*), the nature of the seed-lineage (*gotra-bīja*), the indestructible nature, the nature of the path-seed (*mārga-bīja*), or the nature of the True Dharma (*saddharma*). Within these, [one remains ignorant].
To some extent, they may practice meditative cultivation and emerge from the eighty factors of dhyāna;

yet, regarding each and every dharma of all modes of conduct, they fail to grasp the essential meaning within these teachings. For the sake of gain and fame, they seek and crave excessively, greedily pursuing disciples.
They falsely pretend to understand all the sūtras and vinayas merely for the sake of offerings. Thus, they deceive themselves and likewise deceive others.
If one intentionally bestows the precepts upon another person, one commits a minor offense (light defilement).

Regarding the three stages of the introductory matters: first, clarifying what is understood; because one understands this, one is qualified to be a teacher. Furthermore, it is stipulated that if one does not understand, one commits an offense.
There are three types of obstacles to the Path (*āvaraṇa*): first, the seven grave transgressions (*ānantarya*); second, the twenty heavy offenses; and third, the eighteen light offenses.

Regarding these three matters, each should be thoroughly understood; one who does not wish to accept them must not be coerced, for there is the offense of forcing someone to accept what they do not desire.
If one does not understand the Mahāyāna, this constitutes the second point of failure. Furthermore, acting as a teacher while lacking such understanding is also subject to restraint.
Finally, the third point cites the improper conduct of a bodhisattva to define the nature of the transgression.
Forty-second: Preaching the precepts to evil persons. Generally, those who have not yet received the Bodhisattva precepts are called "evil persons.

If one were to preach [the precepts] to them beforehand, they would be unable to receive them with sincere gravity once they do receive them later; therefore, it is prescribed that all seven groups of followers commit this offense equally, and it is regulated for both major and minor precepts alike.

If a Buddha’s disciple, for the sake of profit and sustenance, should preach these Great Precepts of the Thousand Buddhas before those who have not yet received the Bodhisattva precepts, or before non-Buddhists and evil persons, or even before those with false views, they shall not do so.
With the exception of kings, no other person whatsoever may preach them to such evil people; those who do not receive the Buddha’s precepts are called "beasts."
If one is born in a place where the Three Jewels are not seen, being like wood or stone and devoid of mind, such a person is called a follower of external paths and those with false views;
they are no different from a block of wood. Yet, if a Bodhisattva preaches the teachings and precepts of the Seven Buddhas before such evil persons, they commit a minor offense (light defilement).
The introductory section concerning the three stages: first, one must not speak [of this] lightly;

this excludes only kings, non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*), and evil persons—by which "evil persons" are meant the ninety-five types of heterodox practitioners. Second, those who do not receive [the teaching] are all considered evil persons;
they live in vain and die in vain, being no different from animals. Third, the text cites these failings to bind [the listener] with the fault of transgression.

○ The forty-third precept: Regarding the offense of receiving offerings without shame. Having committed a transgression according to the specific category, one does not reflect upon it with shame or remorse, yet brazenly accepts beneficial offerings.

Because there is no sense of shame, this rule was established. It applies equally to all five groups of the ordained, both great and small, because such conduct wrongs those who are worthy fields of merit (*puṇyakṣetra*).
As the text says: "Those who have left the household life with faith but violate the true precepts [are like those] remaining at home."
If a disciple of the Buddha has left the household life out of faith and received the Buddha’s true precepts, yet conceives a mind to violate these holy precepts,
they shall not receive the offerings of any donors, nor shall they walk upon the ground of the king, nor shall they drink from the kingdom’s [waters].
Five thousand great rākṣasas, as fierce as the water of royal power, constantly block his path. These spirits say, "Great thief!
Whenever he enters a room, a city, or a house, the spirits further sweep away his footprints. All people in the world revile him, saying, "A thief within the Buddha-dharma!
No sentient being wishes to see such a person who violates the precepts; he is no different from a beast or a head of wood."
If one deliberately destroys the right precepts, one commits a secondary offense of light defilement.
Regarding the sequence of matters, there are three layers; the first concerns the offense of being shameless and not receiving offerings.
Kings originally grant land and water to those who possess virtue; those without virtuous conduct should not enjoy such things. (The end of the fifth thousand verses, second layer.)
If one who is guilty and shameless is reviled by ghosts and spirits, this constitutes the third instance of violating the precepts; it identifies the transgression and binds the fault. Forty-fourth:
The Precept Regarding Failure to Make Offerings to the Scriptures, the Dharma, and the Sangha. All three jewels should be honored with offerings;

if one fails to practice this, it contravenes the mind of reverence. Therefore, it is prescribed that all seven assemblies of the ordained and laity commit the same offense, though the gravity of the transgression varies between the Mahayana and Hinayana traditions.
A Bodhisattva should practice five matters; as for the light and heavy rules of the five categories of the Śrāvakas, they should be recited and upheld, while other matters are not prescribed.

If a disciple of the Buddha, he should always with a single mind receive, uphold, read, and recite the Mahāyāna sūtras and vinayas, even if it means flaying his own skin to make paper and piercing [his body]...
Using blood as ink and marrow as water, with bones split to form brushes, one shall write out the Buddha’s precepts upon tree bark, rice paper, silk, or bamboo slips;

these should all be written and maintained. One should always use the seven treasures, priceless incense and flowers, and all manner of miscellaneous jewels to fashion cases and bags to store the volumes of the Sūtras and Vinaya.
If one fails to provide such proper offerings, one commits a minor offense.
The introduction to the matter has three stages: first, the general exhortation to receive and uphold [the teaching]; second, the specific enumeration of five types of exhortations to practice:

first, receiving and upholding; second, reading; third, reciting; fourth, transcribing; and fifth, making offerings. The explanation of these has already been provided above in the thirty-ninth section.
If one does not do so, the third point follows: to cite the wrong and conclude with the fault—that this scripture is the Mother of Buddhas and should be honored with offerings.
Failure to do so constitutes an offense.

○ Forty-fifth: The Precept Against Failing to Transform Sentient Beings. When a Bodhisattva resolves their mind for the sake of others, they should transform all classes of conscious beings, causing them to attain awakening and understanding; if they fail to do so, they deviate from the conduct of a Great Being.

Therefore, it is established that for the seven classes of followers, there are offenses common to all, whether major or minor, as well as those not shared among them. For a Mahāsattva, transforming sentient beings is the correct practice;
for one of the Lesser Vehicle who seeks only self-deliverance and does not transform others, this is not an offense.
If, O Sons of the Buddha, you constantly give rise to the mind of great compassion, and upon entering any city, town, or house, you see any sentient being...
One should proclaim: "All you sentient beings, you must all receive the three refuges and the ten precepts.
If one sees cattle, horses, pigs, sheep, or any other animals, one should mentally reflect and verbally declare: "You are animals; arouse the bodhicitta!
Furthermore, wherever a Bodhisattva enters—be it mountains, forests, rivers, or fields—they cause all sentient beings therein to arouse the bodhicitta.
If this bodhisattva does not give rise to the mind to teach and transform sentient beings, they commit a minor offense (light defilement).
Regarding the introductory matter, there are three layers: first, the exhortation to arouse great compassion; second, the prohibition against failing to do so;

and third, the fact that a Great Being capable of uprooting suffering constantly vows that sentient beings be freed from suffering. If one enters into all [subsequent sections], the following two list the matters concerning the compassionate mind; in total, there are three.

There are two interpretations regarding the first type: causing human beings to receive the Three Refuges and the Ten Precepts—namely, (1) the ten precepts of the Śrāvaka, and (2) the ten grave precepts of the Bodhisattva.
Regarding the second type: causing non-human beings to resolve their minds [toward enlightenment]. Third:

wherever one goes and whomever one encounters, causing all such people to resolve their minds [toward enlightenment]. These three are the urgent necessities for the essential path; they are the universal regulations that govern the Way.
If a lay bodhisattva does not descend [from their seat] during the third formal accusation (*tri-karma*), it is not considered a formal transgression (*āpatti*).

○ The forty-sixth precept, regarding preaching the Dharma in an improper manner: because the person before one is improper yet one forcefully provides an explanation, both parties incur the fault of arrogance toward the Dharma;
therefore, this is established as a rule for the five groups of the ordained, with the same prohibitions for both the Great and Small Vehicles.
If one who lives at home does not act as a full master of the Dharma, even to speak a single sentence or a single verse that is not in accordance with the Dharma constitutes an offense.

If a disciple of the Buddha constantly teaches and transforms others, giving rise to a heart of great compassion, when entering the homes of wealthy patrons or among all assemblies, he must not stand to preach the Dharma to laypeople;
rather, he should sit upon a high seat before the assembly of laypeople in accordance with the Dharma.

A preceptor bhikṣu must not stand upon the ground while preaching the Dharma to the fourfold assembly. When preaching, the Dharma master shall occupy a high seat and be honored with incense and flowers;

the members of the fourfold assembly who listen shall remain seated on lower seats. They should be as filial toward their parents and as respectful and obedient toward their teacher’s instructions as a Brahmin who serves the sacrificial fire.
If the one who preaches the Dharma speaks in a manner that does not accord with the Dharma, they commit a minor offense (light defilement).
The introductory matter has three layers: first, one should always respond with great compassion to transform others, which simultaneously constitutes a regulation;

second, one must not stand to preach the Dharma or establish formal rules for laypeople; third, when preaching to them, one should sit together with them—if both stand together, it is not a transgression.
Here, "standing" is used as a general term; if the person is lying down while the master of the Dharma sits or stands, or...
Furthermore, one must not preach to the fourfold assembly while covering one’s head or holding a staff; nor should one preach while leaning against something.
One must not say, "The monks and nuns possess the Way," and then lean against something while preaching, for this is a disparagement of the Dharma and constitutes an offense.
As for those who preach the Dharma, three instances of such misconduct do not constitute a formal transgression.
○ Forty-seventh: Regarding the precept on illegal restrictions—since one sees a virtuous deed, the Dharma dictates that one should rejoice in it;
yet now, by establishing a restrictive net, one obstructs and hinders it, which contradicts the principle of assisting in goodness.

Therefore, this regulation is established such that both groups of the laity commit the same offense, while for the five groups of renunciants, there is no regulation regarding lack of autonomy. Even if one were to establish a restriction that hinders virtue, it would be governed by the same rule as this.
Whether great or small, all commit the same offense. If, O sons of the Buddha, those who have received the Buddha’s precepts with faith— whether they be kings, crown princes, officials,
or disciples of the fourfold assembly— rely on their own high status to destroy the Buddha-dharma and its precepts, openly establishing restrictive laws to constrain the fourfold assembly;
It is not permitted for disciples to refuse ordination and the practice of the Way, nor is it permitted to refuse the creation of images, stupas, and the scriptures of the Vinaya;
nor is it permitted to establish official systems of administration to control the assembly and require monks to register their names in ledgers.

For Bodhisattvas and Bhikṣus to occupy high seats while laypeople stand below is a widespread practice of unrighteousness, like that of soldiers or slaves serving their masters. In truth, Bodhisattvas should rightly receive the offerings of all people.
Yet, on the contrary, one acts as a servant for officials, violating both the Dharma and the Vinaya.

If kings or the hundred officials who have sincerely received the Buddha’s precepts do not commit such an act, they shall avoid the sin of destroying the Triple Gem; if they intentionally destroy the Dharma, they commit a secondary offense (light impurity).

The introductory matter consists of three stages: first, the designation of the recipient of the precepts; second, the two interpretations thereof. One interpretation states that this designates the person subject to the regulation:
a son of the Buddha who desires to receive the precepts with faith is restricted by obstacles and is not permitted to receive them.

The second interpretation states that this designates the person who establishes the regulation: when a son of the Buddha first receives the precepts with faith, he does not immediately establish unlawful restrictions.
Therefore, it is shown that if one prohibits those below the rank of a king from leaving the household life, this severs the Jewel of the Sangha;
if one does not permit the fourfold assembly—namely laymen, laywomen, boys, and girls—to leave the household life, this severs the Jewel of the Sangha;
if one does not permit the creation of images, this severs the Jewel of the Buddha; and if one does not permit the copying of the sutras and vinaya, this severs the Jewel of the Dharma.
Therefore, the following section is presented to raise objections and point out errors.
○ Forty-eighth: Regarding the "Breaking of the Dharma and Precepts," when members of the community commit transgressions, they should be dealt with according to internal regulations.

To instead disclose their offenses to laypeople or outsiders, thereby subjecting them to punishment by secular law and bringing disgrace upon the pure transformation [of the Sangha], is called "breaking" [the precepts].

Because their practice deviates from the mind that protects the Dharma, it is ordained that the five groups of monastics shall equally refrain from offenses according to both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna codes.

If a disciple of the Buddha has left the household life with a sincere heart, yet for the sake of fame and profit preaches the Buddha’s precepts before kings and officials, and arbitrarily imposes restrictive constraints upon bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, or disciples of the bodhisattva precepts; [this is a transgression].
It is like the law for prisoners or the law for soldiers and slaves; it is like worms within the body of a lion eating the lion’s own flesh, rather than other external insects.
In this way, it is the sons of the Buddha who destroy the Buddha-dharma themselves, not external paths or celestial Māras.
Those who cherish the Buddha's precepts should protect them as one would care for an only child or serve one's parents; they must never be violated or destroyed.
When a Bodhisattva hears the sound of non-Buddhists or evil persons slandering and violating the Buddha’s precepts with wicked words,
it is no different from three hundred spears piercing the heart or thousands of swords and ten thousand clubs striking and beating their body;
they would rather enter hell and remain there for a hundred kalpas than once hear the sound of evil persons slandering and violating the Buddha’s precepts with wicked words.
How much more so when one breaks the Buddha’s precepts oneself and teaches others to break the Dharma; such causes and conditions lack even the heart of filial piety.
If one intentionally commits such acts, one incurs a minor offense (light垢罪).
Regarding the three stages of the introductory matters: first, one must not destroy the Dharma; second, it clarifies the protection of the Dharma, starting from receiving the Buddha’s [teachings].
The text following "this is it" constitutes the third section, which cites instances of wrongdoing and concludes with the transgression of instructing others to destroy the Dharma;
alternatively, this precept may be termed the "precept against causing others to suffer harm."
These nine precepts should be studied and upheld with a reverent heart.
O sons of the Buddha, these forty-eight minor precepts are to be received and maintained by you;
the Bodhisattvas of the past have already recited them, those of the future shall recite them, and the Bodhisattvas of the present are now reciting them.
The third section, "General Conclusion," is divided into three parts: first, the enumeration of the number; second, the exhortation to uphold; and third, the exhortation to recite.

First, the enumeration of the number refers to the forty-eight minor transgressions. "You all should receive and uphold them" constitutes the second part, the exhortation to uphold them within one's mind.
The third part, the exhortation to recite, cites the practice of Bodhisattvas of the three periods as an encouragement to do so.
△ Listen, all you sons of the Buddha! This concludes the third major section on the circulation [of the text]. Within this, it is further divided into two parts:
first, the circulation of the gravity and lightness of these precepts; second, the circulation of this specific chapter.

"O sons of the Buddha, listen attentively! These ten grave and forty-eight light precepts have been recited by all Buddhas of the three periods of time—those who have recited them in the past, those who will recite them in the future, and those who are reciting them now. I now likewise recite them.

You, the entire great assembly—including kings, princes, officials, bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, and laymen and laywomen who have received and uphold the Bodhisattva precepts—should likewise receive and uphold them."

By reading, reciting, understanding, and copying this scroll of the eternally abiding Buddha-nature precepts, you shall cause them to circulate through the three periods of time for all sentient beings, so that their manifestations continue without end.
You shall behold a thousand Buddhas, and as each Buddha extends a hand to you, you shall never fall into the evil realms or the eight difficulties in successive lifetimes;
instead, you shall always be born among humans or in the heavens. Now, beneath this tree, I have briefly expounded for you the Dharma-precepts of the seven Buddhas.

The great assembly should with one mind study the Prātimokṣa and joyfully practice it, as is extensively clarified in each instance within the "Exhortation to Study" chapter of the *Animitta-devaputra-parivarta*.
At that time, the three thousand scholars seated there listening heard the Buddha recite it himself;
they received it upon their hearts with reverence, receiving and upholding it with joy.
Regarding the first point—the circulation of these precepts—there are four further intentions: first, the recitation; second, the formal circulation;
third, the benefits gained from circulation; and fourth, the observance by the great assembly. Within these four, each has three further distinctions.
Regarding the first, the recitation, there are three parts: first, the designation of the title; second, the recitation by the Buddhas of the three periods; and third, my own recitation as Śākyamuni.
The first recitation, consisting of several tens of repetitions of the titles, concerns the forty-eight minor transgressions.
The second [recitation] is the exhortation to uphold and maintain this precept, as it is revered by all Buddhas of the three periods of time.
The third is my own recitation as Śākyamuni, intended to circulate [the teaching] and exhort sentient beings. Among these four stages, "you, the entire assembly," refers to the second stage.
The circulation [of this teaching] also has three aspects: first, the person who circulates it; second, the manner of circulation; and third, the matter of circulation.
Regarding the person who circulates it, this refers to the great assembly present here. Regarding the manner of circulation, it refers to the five kinds of Dharma-preachers.

Regarding the matter of circulation, it means that by means of these precepts and dharmas, the transmission flows through the three periods of time, with transformation following transformation without end, such that one may come to behold a thousand Buddhas.
This concludes the third stage among the four stages of circulation and benefit. The benefit consists in seeing one thousand Buddhas. Regarding this text, there are three points:
first, encountering the Sages; second, being freed from suffering; and third, attaining happiness. "Encountering the Sages" refers to seeing one thousand Buddhas.
While the Buddhas of the three periods all appear to the vision, here only those of a single period are mentioned; for every Buddha, [the same applies].

"Extending the hand" does not mean merely raising the hand to offer it; it clarifies that one who upholds the precepts according to the Dharma is as close to the Buddha as a neighbor—so near that there is no distance between them—and thus, in this sense, it is called "extending the hand.
This means that in every lifetime one shall not fall away and will be separated from suffering, while constantly being born into states of happiness.
What is avoided and what is attained cannot be limited to these alone; rather, I have cited here those things generally favored or loathed by ordinary beings.
This is merely for the purpose of encouragement. I am now here beneath this tree entrusting [this teaching] for its practice; what follows below shall not be further expounded.
At that time, Śākyamuni Buddha spoke these words at the request of Vairocana Buddha in the world-system of the Lotus Flower Terrace Treasury.
The section on the Ten Inexhaustible Precepts within the "Chapter on the Dharma-Gate of the Mind-Ground" is concluded. The thousand billion Śākyamunis likewise spoke this;

from the palace of the Heavenly King Maheśvara down to this site beneath the Bodhi tree, these ten stages of dwelling in the teaching of the Dharma have been expounded for the sake of the unspeakably vast assembly of all bodhisattvas, who shall uphold, read, recite, and explain their meaning.

In the same way, throughout the hundreds of thousands of millions of worlds—the worlds as numerous as the atoms within the Lotus Treasury World—all Buddhas have completed the preaching of all the infinite treasuries of Dharma:

This is merely an incomplete excerpt, consisting of four stages and one partial summary: (1) the *Cittabhūmi-varga* (Chapter on the Ground of Mind); (2) a brief enumeration and general conclusion regarding the ten locations;
(3) the Dharma taught; and (4) the practice by the great assembly. The first stage has two distinct parts: (1) clarifying the end of what was spoken by this Śākyamuni;
and (2) clarifying the end of what was spoken by other Śākyamunis. From the second [stage], starting with Maheśvara...
The third stage concludes the exposition of the ten points; it is also twofold. First, it cites these ten points taught by Śākyamuni from the upper fascicle.
Second, it cites other teachings spoken by Śākyamuni; the end of the text concerning these other teachings of Śākyamuni is likewise missing, and one should study them in this manner.
The third stage cites the teachings spoken, totaling seven phrases; it is also twofold: the first six are specific, and the last one is general.
This summarizes the fourth great assembly throughout the thousands of billions of worlds, who likewise practice as previously clarified;
it also indicates that within each of those thousands of billions of worlds, sentient beings each speak and each practice.

For a more detailed exposition, one should refer to the "Chapter on the Buddha Flower-Light King" (*Buddhavaipulya-sūtra*), which should be the Great Version (*Mahāvaipulya*). This version differs from the [text based on] the three thousand [worlds].
This refers to the three thousand modes of deportment that a bodhisattva should study for three years; whereas for śrāvakas it is five years, for bodhisattvas it is three years.
The three matters are precept, concentration, and wisdom.
One who possesses clear understanding and strong patience and wisdom can uphold such a Dharma until they attain the path of Buddhahood.
One securely obtains five kinds of benefits: First, the Buddhas of the ten directions Compassionately regard and constantly protect one.
Second, at the time of death, With right view, the mind is filled with joy. Third, in every place of rebirth, one becomes A companion to all bodhisattvas.
Fourth, the accumulation of merit— The perfection of ethical discipline—is fully accomplished.
Fifth: In this life and in future lives, may the nature-precepts, merit, and wisdom be fulfilled. This is the sphere of the Buddha’s practice;
let the wise contemplate it well. Those who calculate in terms of a self and cling to signs cannot believe in this Dharma.
Even those who have attained the realization of extinction are not the ground for planting seeds if they wish to grow the sprouts of Bodhi.
The radiance illuminates the world; one should contemplate it with stillness.
The true nature of all phenomena is neither arising nor ceasing, Neither eternal nor annihilated, neither identical nor different, Neither coming nor going.
Within this single mind, One should diligently adorn it through skillful means.
What a bodhisattva ought to do should be learned in its proper sequence;
one should not give rise to conceptual distinctions regarding those in training or those beyond training. This is called the foremost path, and it is also called the Mahāyāna.
All evil conceptual proliferations are extinguished from this very source, as is the *sarvajñatā* (all-knowledge) of all Buddhas.
All [qualities] emerge from this source; therefore, O sons of the Buddha, you should arouse great courage regarding the pure precepts of the Buddhas and protect them as if they were a bright pearl.
The Bodhisattvas of the past have already trained in this, those of the future shall train in it, and those of the present are training in it now.
This is the sphere of the Buddha’s activity, praised by the Holy Lord.
Having followed [the teaching] and spoken thus, may this immeasurable mass of merit be dedicated to all sentient beings;
may those who hear this Dharma together with me swiftly attain the path of Buddhahood.

The *Tiantai Jieshu* (Commentary on the Precepts) by the same [author] has long been circulated in the world; however, as the scripture and its commentary were transmitted separately, there are many discrepancies and omissions.

This has caused both lecturers and students to suffer from its deficiencies. Lately, disregarding my own lack of talent, I have collated ancient manuscripts and compared them with those preserved in the Tripitaka;
having thus reconciled the text, I entrusted it to the carvers to ensure its circulation.
This was done because I, too, had previously suffered from these same difficulties, hoping that the light of the Perfect and Sudden Precepts might once again shine brightly through this endeavor.
